title: Latest macOS beta: What’s new and should you install it?
content:
Macworld





Apple released macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14, 2026, but development hasn’t stopped. Just two days later on September 16, Apple issued the first developer beta of macOS 27.2, beginning testing of the operating system’s next major point update. Yes, that’s macOS 27.2, not macOS 27.1. 
The macOS 27.2 beta gives developers and testers early access to Apple’s latest fixes, refinements and any features that weren’t ready for the initial Golden Gate release. 
However, as with any beta software, it may introduce bugs, compatibility problems and poorer battery life so we recommend caution if you wish to install it.
Here’s everything you need to know about the latest macOS beta, including what’s new, when the next public beta is likely to arrive and whether you should install it.


What’s the latest macOS beta? 
Apple offers two beta streams: a developer beta and a public beta. The public beta allows enthusiasts and early adopters to test upcoming changes before they are released to everyone. You need to join Apple’s Beta Software Program to access it.
The latest Mac beta is macOS 27.2 beta 3, which Apple released to registered developers on October 5, 2026.
The corresponding macOS 27.2 public beta will be available soon. Public betas usually follow developer betas, although Apple does not guarantee a particular schedule.
macOS 27 Golden Gate beta version tracker 
Apple released macOS 27.2 Golden Gate Developer Beta 3 on October 5, 2026.
The macOS 27.2 Golden Gate Public Beta 2 arrived on September 22; new versions are usually released a day or two after the new developer beta.
macOS 26 Tahoe beta: Apple may continue updating macOS 26 Tahoe with security and maintenance releases, but macOS 27 is now the current operating system and the focus of Apple’s beta program.

What’s new in the latest beta?

				
					

				
			
New features in macOS 27.

Foundry




Apple has not announced any major consumer-facing additions in macOS 27.2 beta 2. The following changes are expected though:
Bug fixes and performance improvements: Addressing issues in the first release of macOS 27.
Additional Siri AI languages: Apple has said the Siri AI will expand to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish in October. 
Automatic password changes: The promised feature that automatically changes compromised passwords has not yet been implemented, but it could arrive in macOS 27.2.. 
We’ll update this section as changes are discovered.
See Apple’s developer website for more information about the beta. 


						

							


Should you install the macOS beta?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Installing the macOS beta lets you test Apple’s next round of features, fixes and refinements before their public release. Most Mac users should remain on the standard version of macOS 27, particularly if they rely on their Mac for work.
Install if…
You need to test apps
You want early access to new features
You have a secondary Mac available
Wait if…
This is your primary work machine
You rely on niche or specialist software
Stability is critical to your workflow


						

							






Who are you Should you install?

A developer testing appsConsider the developer beta
An enthusiast with a spare MacConsider the public beta 
General user with one MacStay on macOS 27

 






What are the risks of installing beta software?
Installing pre-release software on a primary device carries several risks.
System instability: Performance problems, freezes, crashes, and other unexpected behavior are common during beta testing.
App failures: Third-party applications may crash, behave unpredictably, or stop working entirely.
Hardware strain: Early beta builds can increase battery drain and cause Macs to run hotter than usual.
Data loss: Software bugs may corrupt files, and downgrading to a stable version often requires a complete system reset.


						

							


Safety precautions and best practices
If you decide to install the beta, take the following precautions:
Use a secondary device: Avoid installing beta software on your primary Mac or on any machine used for critical work.
Create a full backup: Use Time Machine to create a complete backup before upgrading so you can restore your Mac if something goes wrong. Note that this needs to be a Time Machine backup from before the beta was installed and you will lose anything saved subsequently.
Install on a separate volume: Consider installing the beta on a separate volume or external SSD rather than replacing your main operating system.
Check storage space: Make sure you have at least 15GB of free storage available before beginning the installation.


						

							


How to install the macOS beta

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The process for installing a macOS beta depends on whether you are seeking the Developer Beta or the Public Beta. Apple simplified this process a few years ago, removing the need for a paid developer account to access early builds. 
The first step is to join Apple’s beta testing program. We explain how to do that in a separate article.
You will need to register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac.
To install the beta follow these steps:
Back up your Mac: Before installing any pre-release software, it is critical to prepare your Mac to avoid data loss. Beta software is inherently unstable and can cause crashes or app compatibility issues. 
Register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac:
For the Public Beta: Visit the Apple Beta Software Program website, sign in with your Apple ID, and agree to the terms.
For the Developer Beta: Register as an Apple Developer on Apple’s website, download the Apple Developer app from the App Store, sign in with your standard Apple ID, and complete the free registration process.
On the Mac where you wish to install the beta, open System Settings and navigate to General > Software Update.
Click the (i) info button next to Beta Updates.
Enable Beta Updates.
The beta will appear as an available upgrade. Select the macOS beta you want to install (e.g., macOS Public Beta or Developer Beta).
Click Upgrade Now to begin the download and installation.
As long as you are a registered developer or enrolled in the public beta program, when the relevant macOS Beta becomes available, it will also show up on your Mac.
Once you are running the beta, the updates will come through to your Mac automatically; you just need to go to Software Update in System Settings and click to install. See How to install macOS.


						

							


How to get a free Apple developer account
If you just want a free Apple Developer account so you can access the beta, you can get this via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app on an iPhone:
Get the Apple Developer App from the App Store. 
Open the app on your iPhone. 
Tap on Account. 
Tap on Sign In. 
Sign in using your usual Apple ID. 
If you wish to actually publish applications to the App Store or receive support, you’ll need to pay $99/£79 per year for a paid account. You can compare the free and paid accounts here.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
Who can run the macOS beta?
Anyone can run the macOS beta, but to do so, you do need to register for either the developer beta, the public beta, or both.
Apple offers both developer and public beta programs for macOS, enabling all interested users to test pre-release versions of the operating system. While both betas provide early access to new features, they cater to different user profiles based on technical expertise and risk tolerance. Beta software tends to be buggy so the more stable public beta version may be preferable, but even that will not be bug-free.
In the past, the developer beta was only available to developers who had paid to join Apple’s Developer Program (which costs $99/£79). However, for a couple of years now, Apple has opened up the developer beta to registered developers with free developer accounts. We explain how to get a free developer account below. 
If you decide you no longer want to run the beta version of macOS read this: How to remove the macOS beta.





2.
macOS public beta vs developer beta
Since 2023, the Developer Beta has been available to anyone who registers as a developer, even if they aren’t a paid-up member of Apple’s Developer Program. As a result, people with a basic free developer account can download the new macOS developer beta (we show you how to register below).
Whether you should download the developer beta if you aren’t a developer is another question. We don’t recommend you install the developer beta if you aren’t a developer. Instead, our recommendation is to use the public beta (the first version of which usually arrives in July).
There are a few differences between the public and developer betas. The public beta is not the same as the beta that is released through the developer program. The public beta typically launches after the developer beta has undergone initial testing and refinement
Developers get updates to their beta first, and possibly more frequently. But you should keep in mind that betas are by nature not stable, and because the public beta comes after the developer beta it could be a little safer to install. 
The most significant difference is probably the motive of the testers: Developers usually have the aim of ensuring their apps work when the updated macOS is released to the general public, while public beta testers are essentially helping Apple detect bugs and offering feedback on the features. Because of this, developers may get to test new features not available in the public beta. 
If you want to get the public beta the first thing you need to do, if you haven’t already, is join Apple’s beta programs read this for more information: How to become an Apple beta tester.





3.
Is the macOS beta stable?
By its nature, a beta has the potential to be unstable. Therefore, it’s not advised that you install it on a Mac that you rely on. If you have a second Mac that isn’t mission-critical, then install it there. We strongly recommend that you don’t risk all by putting the macOS beta on your primary Mac, especially not in the early days of the beta development. 
If you don’t have a second Mac, there are a couple of ways you could run macOS beta on your Mac without running the risk of losing data or finding your Mac stops working:
We recommend installing it on a partition, which these days is really a volume (and is much easier to create than a partition was). Read about how to do that here: How to dual-boot Mac: Run two versions of macOS on a Mac.
Alternatively, you could install the macOS beta on an external drive and run it on that.
We discuss the safety of the macOS beta and the risks you might be taking in more detail in a separate article.





4.
How to prepare your Mac for the beta
Update your software: We recommend you have the latest full version of macOS installed, although Apple says that the macOS Developer Beta Access Utility requires macOS 10.8 or later.
Make space: We’d recommend at least 25-30GB of available space because the macOS betas tend to be very large. If you end up requiring more space, read: How to free up space on Mac. Note that we always recommend that you have at least 10% space free on your Mac at any time, so if you don’t have that, expect problems!
Back up: Before you install a beta on your Mac, you should make a backup of your data and files. You can find out how to use Time Machine to back up your Mac. We also have a round-up of suitable backup solutions.





5.
How to send feedback to Apple
Should you come across an error or a bug, you should use the Feedback Assistant app to provide feedback to Apple. Launch the app and follow the appropriate steps, selecting the area about which you’re providing feedback and then any specific sub-area. Then describe your issue in a single sentence, before providing a more detailed description, including any specific steps that reproduce the issue. You’ll also be able to attach other files.
You’ll also have to give permission for the Feedback Assistant app to collect diagnostic information from your Mac.
It won’t always be obvious whether something is a bug or just not as easy to use as you might have hoped. Either way, if your feedback is that something appears to work in an illogical way, Apple will want to know that.
If you are having trouble with a third-party app, you can let Apple know by reporting it through the 3rd-party Application Compatibility category in the Feedback Assistant. However, we’d suggest that you also provide feedback to the app’s developer, who will no doubt be grateful.





6.
Will I be able to update from macOS beta to the final version?
Beta users can move to the finished release once its build is newer than – or equivalent to – the beta installed. Read: How to leave the macOS beta.  





7.
Can I talk about the beta publicly?
According to Apple and the license agreement all beta testers must agree to, the beta is “Apple confidential information”. By accepting those terms, you agree not to discuss your use of the software with anyone who isn’t also in the Beta Software Program. That means you can’t “blog, post screenshots, tweet, or publicly post information about the public beta software.”
However, you can discuss any information that Apple has publicly disclosed; the company says that information is no longer considered confidential.





8.
How to downgrade from the macOS beta
You can always revert to an earlier version of macOS, though depending on how you back up, it’s not necessarily a painless process.
Start by making sure the data on your drive is backed up, then erase the drive and install the latest public version of macOS. When you first start up your Mac, you can use the Migration Assistant to import your data from the backup. Here’s a more detailed tutorial on downgrading from the macOS beta and we also have a tutorial on downgrading to an older version of the Mac OS.





9.
Is the beta free to download? 
Yes, the macOS beta is free to download for both developers and the general public. Apple offers two distinct tracks for testing pre-release software: the Developer Beta and the Public Beta, both of which are now accessible without a paid subscription.





10.
Can I go back to the stable version?
Yes, you can go back to the stable version of macOS from a beta, but the complexity of the process depends on whether the final version of that software has been released yet.
If you are running macOS 27.2 beta and want to return to the current public release of macOS 27, simply turning off Beta Updates will stop future beta installations, but it will not immediately downgrade the Mac. To return before Apple releases an equivalent public build, you may need to erase the Mac and reinstall macOS, then restore data from a backup made before installing the beta.





11.
Should I install the beta on my main Mac?
Installing a macOS beta on your primary computer is generally not recommended due to the inherent risks of using unfinished software. While beta programs offer early access to new features, they are designed for testing and often contain significant bugs that can disrupt your daily workflow.





12.
Do I need an Apple Developer account to install the beta?
You do not need a paid Apple Developer account to install the macOS beta. While access to developer betas was previously restricted to those paying a $99/£79 annual fee, Apple changed this policy in 2023 to allow anyone with a free developer account to access these builds. Alternatively, you can join the Public Beta program, which is also free and accessible to anyone with a valid Apple ID.





13.
How often are new beta versions released?
New macOS beta versions are typically released every one to two weeks, with the frequency increasing as the final public release date approaches. The beta updates refine features and address bugs identified by testers.





14.
Is the macOS beta safe to install?
The beta is generally safe to test, but it may contain bugs that cause crashes, poor battery life, app compatibility issues, or data loss. Always back up your Mac before installing.





15.
Will my apps work with the macOS beta?
Many apps will work normally, but some third-party software may crash, perform poorly, or not launch at all until developers release updates.

title: macOS development continues to hint at touchscreen MacBooks
content:
Apple's latest macOS 27.2 beta references new touch gestures for Safari and Notes, meaning we're in for a neat Sidecar upgrade, a touchscreen MacBook Pro, or both.


macOS 27.2 beta 3 includes new touchscreen gestures for system apps.
While rumors of a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen go back years, it looks as though the device is finally nearing release. Monday's macOS 27.2 beta indicates that multiple system applications will receive additional touch recognition capabilities.
As MacRumors points out, the Notes app supports a feature dubbed "ICTouchPressGestureRecognizer," while QuickLook gained a "dragTouch" capability. Safari, meanwhile, was updated with a "touch sentinel recognizer," though these capabilities are only referenced in the software code.

title: tvOS 27.2 Code Hints at Apple Intelligence for New Apple TV
content:
Apple's latest tvOS 27.2 beta adds weight to rumors that the next Apple TV will have Siri AI and Apple Intelligence support. Code suggests Apple is adding an Improve ‌Siri‌ & ‌Apple Intelligence‌ toggle to the tvOS Settings app.


"Help improve foundation models and ‌Siri‌ by allowing Apple to collect and use your text and audio interactions with ‌Siri‌, Dictation, and Translate," the text reads.

Other Apple devices with ‌Apple Intelligence‌ have similarly labeled privacy disclosures and data-sharing opt-ins. On devices that don't support ‌Apple Intelligence‌, the setting is labeled "Improve ‌Siri‌ & Dictation." The new code is included alongside the existing code for ‌Siri‌ data sharing, so it's likely only Apple Intelligence-capable hardware will see it.

tvOS 27.2 also has a new ‌Siri‌ Messages UI framework, indicating message content could be displayed on the ‌Apple TV‌ in the future. ‌Siri‌ may be able to read messages sent to a linked iPhone and show smart reply options on the ‌Apple TV‌. The current version of ‌Siri‌ on ‌Apple TV‌ doesn't support sending or reading messages, so the framework is likely linked to ‌Siri‌ AI.

title: macOS 27.2 Adds Touch Gestures Ahead of MacBook Ultra
content:
macOS Golden Gate 27.2 adds code referencing new touch-specific gestures in apps like Safari, Notes, Photos, and Quick Look, a possible sign Apple is preparing to release the rumored OLED touchscreen MacBook, possibly called the "MacBook Ultra."


Code in the latest beta adds new gesture recognition tools to several Apple apps. Safari gets a touch sentinel recognizer, ‌Photos‌ has PXGTouchDwellGestureRecognizer, Notes has ICTouchPressGestureRecognizer, and Quick Look gets a dragTouch feature.

Sidecar. ‌macOS Golden Gate‌ brought full touch input to ‌Sidecar‌, which is the feature that lets an iPad be used as a display for a Mac. It's possible Apple is expanding on those ‌Sidecar‌ features, so it's not a clear indication of a new Mac.

Touch-friendly changes started with the launch version of ‌macOS Golden Gate‌, which added pull-to-refresh gestures in Safari, Mail, and Calendar.

MacBook Ultra with touchscreen capabilities could launch as soon as late 2026. The device is rumored to be thinner and lighter than existing models, and it's expected to have a Dynamic Island and Apple's M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

title: Apple and AT&T Have Yet to Explain Cause of iPhone 18 Pro Max Issue
content:
In a statement shared with MacRumors on Friday, Apple said that iPhone 18 Pro Max users who have experienced an issue where AT&T cellular service does not work will need to have the device replaced, as the issue apparently cannot be fixed with a software update once it has occurred. This requirement is a big deal, as it hints at hardware failure, but we lack details since Apple and AT&T have yet to disclose the underlying cause of the issue.


A spokesperson for AT&T directed us to Apple, which has yet to respond to our latest request for comment. It is possible that Apple is still investigating the issue, but so far our follow-up questions have been met with radio silence (pun intended).

iOS 27.0.1 and an AT&T carrier settings update released last week "are meant to help prevent this issue from occurring," so iPhone 18 Pro Max users who have not experienced this issue should ensure that both of these updates are installed immediately to avoid potential future impacts.

To install iOS 27.0.1, open the Settings app on your iPhone and tap General → Software Update. 

The carrier settings update for the iPhone 18 Pro Max will automatically download for AT&T users within the next 14 days, according to Apple. To manually trigger the update, users can open the Settings app and tap General → About.

Apple said it has only observed this issue with iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network. No other iPhone models or carriers are known to be impacted.

rely on Qualcomm's Snapdragon X80 modem for cellular connectivity, while variants of the device sold in all other countries are equipped with Apple's custom C2 modem. It is unclear if this modem difference is a factor in this AT&T issue, or if the overlap is merely a coincidence.

We have reached out to Qualcomm and will share the company's response, if any.

Which AirPods should you buy? 
AirPods 5: Best for buyers who prefer earbuds without silicone tips.

AirPods Max 2: Best for those who specifically want over-ear headphones.
AirPods 4 and AirPods Pro 2: Consider only when clearance prices offer a substantial saving over their replacements.
Apple’s AirPods lineup caters to different priorities, from premium audio and health features to budget-friendly everyday listening. 
AirPods Pro 3: The Best All-Rounder
Released in September 2025, the AirPods Pro 3 are Apple’s flagship earbuds. They combine excellent noise cancellation, improved comfort thanks to foam-infused ear tips, and new health-tracking capabilities. 
AirPods 5: The Budget-Friendly Choice
The AirPods 5 offer a more affordable entry point and are a good choice for anyone who prefers an open-ear design over silicone-tipped earbuds.
AirPods Max 2: Premium Over-Ear Audio
Launched in April 2026, the AirPods Max 2 retain the premium design of the original model while adding Apple’s H2 chip for improved performance and audio processing. 
Still not sure which AirPods to buy? Take a look at our Best AirPods buying guide. Also, if it doesn’t have to be AirPods, take a look at how other over-ears compare to the AirPods Max, and our favorite AirPods alternatives.


						

							


Amazon Prime Day AirPods deals to avoid
Compare older AirPods with the discounted price of their replacements. A large reduction from an old launch price can still represent poor value. Check the generation, charging case, condition and seller before ordering.
Be wary of promotions that advertise “free” AirPods. These offers often require long-term financial commitments or involve complicated rebate processes. For example, a recent Apple Card promotion offered AirPods Pro 3 for signing up, but only through a reimbursement scheme outlined in the fine print.
You should also be cautious with marketplace and third-party sellers offering supposedly new AirPods at prices dramatically below those from established retailers. Counterfeit models are common and are often advertised at discounts far below Apple’s normal pricing. If a deal seems too good to be true, it’s worth checking whether the product is genuine. AirPods Pro and AirPods 4.

As well as getting free two-day shipping, Prime customers also get access to Prime Video and Music.
Alternative Sales: If you miss Prime Day, the Black Friday sales in November will be the next opportunity to get discounts.
Compare Prices: Amazon isn’t always the cheapest option. Retailers such as Walmart and Best Buy frequently run competing “anti-Prime Day” promotions, so it’s worth comparing prices before buying.
Prime Day is available in multiple countries, including Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, Portugal, Singapore, Spain, the U.K., and the U.S.

Which Apple Watch should you buy this Prime Day

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Choosing the right Apple Watch depends on your specific needs, whether you are looking for a rugged outdoor companion, a feature-rich flagship, or a budget-friendly entry point into the ecosystem. Our top recommendation for this Prime Day is the Apple Watch Series 12.
Apple Watch Series 12: Best for most users
Buy the Series 12 if you want Apple’s latest health features without the size and expense of the Ultra. It combines the new Health Sensing System with a 24-hour battery rating and starts at $399/£369.
Apple Watch Ultra 4: Best for endurance and outdoor use
Choose the Ultra 4 if you need 50-hour battery life, satellite connectivity, precision GPS, diving support or extended workout tracking.
Apple Watch SE 3: Best budget option
The SE 3 is the cheapest current Apple Watch and provides most of the core smartwatch, fitness and safety experience. Its main omissions are Apple’s more advanced health sensors.
Series 11 and Ultra 3: Best clearance opportunities
Don’t automatically dismiss last year’s watches. If retailers heavily discount remaining stock, Series 11 and Ultra 3 could offer better value than the new models.
For more advice read our Best Apple Watch guide.  


						

							


Is an older Apple Watch a good Prime Day deal?

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t assume an older Apple Watch is a bad buy. The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are only one generation old and can make excellent buys if they’re substantially cheaper than the Series 12 or Ultra 4.
Be much more cautious with the Series 8, SE 2 and original Ultra, however. Those models cannot run watchOS 27. The Series 9 is the oldest standard Apple Watch compatible with watchOS 27, while the Ultra 2 is the oldest supported Ultra.
Also compare the sale price with the newest equivalent. A $50 Series 11 saving, for example, may not be enough to justify giving up the Series 12’s new health features, whereas a substantially larger saving could change the calculation.
Should you buy GPS or Cellular?
Don’t automatically pay extra for cellular. The Series 12 costs $100/£100 more with cellular, while the SE 3 premium is $50/£70. Cellular is included with every Ultra 4. For many users, GPS is sufficient because the Watch can still track workouts, use Apple Pay and play downloaded music without an iPhone. Cellular becomes most useful if you regularly leave your iPhone behind but still want calls, messages and online services. Read: Do I need a cellular Apple Watch?


						

							


Should you buy an Apple Watch during Amazon Prime Day?
Amazon’s October Prime Day sale is unusually well timed for Apple Watch buyers because Apple’s 2026 models have only just arrived. If the Series 12 or Ultra 4 is discounted, you can buy the newest generation without paying Apple’s full launch price.
It’s also an excellent time to look at previous-generation stock. Series 11 and Ultra 3 are still relatively recent watches, and retailers may discount them aggressively now that their replacements are available.
The other option is to wait until Black Friday in November. If an October deal is modest and you aren’t in a hurry, Black Friday may bring another opportunity – but there’s no guarantee that a particular configuration or older model will remain in stock. Read: When is the best time to buy an Apple Watch?
Before you buy, keep the following in mind:
Prime Membership Requirement: Many of the best deals are exclusive to Amazon Prime members. If you’re not a Prime subscriber, you can take advantage of Amazon’s 30-day free trial or sign up for a month and cancel afterward. Prime membership costs $139 / £95 / AUD$59 annually, or $14.99 / £8.99 / AU$6.99 on a monthly basis. As well as getting free two-day shipping, Prime customers also get access to Prime Video and Music.
Compare Prices: Amazon isn’t always the cheapest retailer. Stores such as Walmart and Best Buy often run competing promotions during Prime Day, so it’s worth checking prices elsewhere before making a purchase.
Alternative Sales: Missed Prime Day? Similar discounts often return during the Black Friday sales in November.
Student Savings: Students may find better value through Apple’s Education Store.  
Prime Day deals are available in multiple countries, including Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, Portugal, Singapore, Spain, the U.K., and the U.S.


						

							


Why you can trust Macworld’s recommendations
We have decades of experience with Apple devices and have tested and reviewed every Apple Watch since the original model. Everything we recommend has been thoroughly tested and weighed against its contemporaries and previous models.
We don’t recommend products we wouldn’t buy, and we don’t point out a deal unless it’s actually a deal—a product that can always be found at the “sale” price really isn’t on sale. Macworld checks Prime Day deals, comparing against MSRP, price history, model relevance and deal quality before we give our recommendation.

title: Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max recall explained: Is Qualcomm to blame?
content:
Macworld





The launch of the iPhone 18 Pro Max has been anything but smooth for AT&T users. Ever since the phone started shipping two weeks ago, reports have been cropping up about an inability to make calls, send texts, or even call emergency services. Considering we’re talking about a phone, it’s a serious issue.
In a statement to Macworld and other media outlets, Apple said that “a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network” with phones that have already been affected by the issue will need to get them replaced. If you bought an AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max, here’s what you need to know.
Update: Added a section explaining whether the problem will definitely be fixed with a replacement phone.
What is the problem?
Apple has identified an issue that specifically stops the iPhone 18 Pro Max from accessing AT&T’s network, preventing users from making calls and sending texts. The smaller iPhone 18 Pro, which was released at the same time, does not exhibit the same issue, nor do iPhone 18 Pro Max devices on Verizon or T-Mobile.
The issue doesn’t appear to affect all AT&T phones, however. While there have been numerous reports from AT&T subscribers with iPhones that haven’t been able to make calls ever since they got the phone, others only experienced the issue after a few days, and still others haven’t had it at all. It’s not clear what triggers the issue.
Can Apple fix it?
Last week, Apple pushed out iOS 27.0.1 to fix a Face ID bug and other launch-day issues with the iPhone 18 Pro Max. The AT&T bug wasn’t listed in the release notes, but AT&T urged its subscribers to install the update as a potential fix. The carrier also pushed out its own update to iPhone 18 Pro Max users that will roll out over the next two weeks.
However, we have since learned that those fixes only prevent the problem from occurring in future; they don’t fix phones that are already exhibiting the issue. In fact, Apple and AT&T both acknowledge that phones with the problem will need to be replaced with a phone that already has iOS 27.0.1 and AT&T’s carrier settings update installed.
Is there an official recall?
Apple has only issued two iPhone recalls in its history, and both offered repairs rather than replacements. In 2021, Apple began a program to fix iPhone 12 or iPhone 12 Pro units that did not emit sound from the receiver when making or receiving calls, and in 2024, iPhone 14 Plus owners who could not see previews when taking photos with the rear camera were also eligible for free repairs.
So, while this is the first time Apple is specifically offering replacement devices, Apple hasn’t declared an official service program. However, if your phone experiences the issue, you should contact AT&T or Apple to swap it out for a new phone.
Will a new phone definitely fix the issue?
It seems as though the problem has been mitigated with a new iPhone 18 Pro Max running iOS 27.0.1 and AT&T’s carrier update. However, Macworld was contacted by a technician familiar with the issue who has dealt with some 50 cases. However, they report that some customers who received replacements still reported frequent outages and issues with cellular connectivity. However, these phones did not have both the iOS update and AT&T’s settings fix applied.
Since AT&T’s fix is rolling out over the coming weeks, it’s possible that a replacement phone will exhibit the same issues. So unless it’s a matter of urgency, it might be better to wait a few days until we have more clarity, or an official statement from Apple.
Why isn’t the iPhone 18 Pro affected?
Neither Apple nor AT&T have divulged the specific issue with the iPhone 18 Pro Max that affects its ability to access data. There’s very little about the phone that isn’t identical to the iPhone 18 Pro other than the size of the screen and battery, but there is one notable component that’s different: the iPhone 18 Pro Max uses a Qualcomm modem rather than an Apple one.
According to teardowns, it’s the same modem as the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, the Snapdragon X80 5G Modem, and neither of those phones exhibit the issue. And even though Apple is offering replacement phones, the issue appears to be a software one related to how the hardware interacts specifically with AT&T’s network.
It’s not clear why the iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple’s most expensive phone that doesn’t fold, uses an older Qualcomm modem in the U.S. rather than Apple’s new C2 modem, which supports mmWave networks for the first time. (In other countries, the 18 Pro Max does have a C2.) Indeed, a lot of older and cheaper iPhones have C-class Apple modems too: last year’s iPhone Air has the C1X, as does the iPhone 17e. The iPhone 16e from February 2025 featured a C1… but the more expensive iPhone 16 has a Qualcomm modem. It’s all quite complicated.
I have an AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max. What should I do?
This depends on whether you’ve experienced the symptoms described above. 
If your iPhone appears to have escaped the bug so far, install iOS 27.0.1 right now. (Open Settings, go to General > Software Update, and follow the prompts.) You’ll also want the latest carrier settings update. This should download automatically within the next 14 days, but you can manually trigger the process by opening Settings and going to General > About.
If you have experienced the problems… well, it’s still worth installing the updates because this is free and takes almost no time. There’s always the extremely slim possibility that you were suffering from an unrelated bug and it may be fixed by a patch or go away by itself. But realistically, you’re going to need a replacement phone. Assuming the problems persist, contact Apple Support or AT&T, or visit an Apple Store or AT&T location.
But your mileage may vary. A reader with one of the affected phones reached out and said he was sent to the Apple Store after trying Best Buy (where he bought the phone) and an AT&T store after neither had any information about the recall. Eventually he found an Apple representative who tested the phone and agreed to ship a replacement device. We expect Apple will announce an official program to address the issue soon.

Which MacBook should you buy?

Apple’s current MacBook range falls into three clear categories:
MacBook Air M5: Best MacBook for most people
The M5 MacBook Air is our default recommendation for most buyers. It combines strong performance, long battery life and portability without the higher price of a MacBook Pro. With no replacement expected until 2027, a good Prime Day discount would be easy to recommend.
MacBook Neo: Best budget MacBook
The MacBook Neo is the cheapest MacBook and is best suited to students and anyone who mainly needs a laptop for web browsing, documents, streaming and video calls. If a discounted MacBook Air is only moderately more expensive, however, the Air is the better long-term buy.
MacBook Pro M5: Best for demanding work
The MacBook Pro is the better choice for video editing, software development, 3D work and other demanding tasks that benefit from sustained performance. Prime Day discounts could be worthwhile, although a redesigned MacBook Pro is rumored before the end of 2026.
MacBook Pro M5 Pro/Max: Best for professional workloads
Choose an M5 Pro or M5 Max model if you need significantly more CPU and GPU performance, additional memory or greater connectivity. If you already own an M4 Pro or M4 Max model, there is little reason to upgrade.
For most Prime Day shoppers, we recommend starting with the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo becomes especially compelling when heavily discounted, while MacBook Pro buyers should consider whether they need the additional performance and professional features enough to justify the considerably higher price.

Mac mini M6: Best desktop for most people
The new M6 Mac mini is our default desktop recommendation. It starts at $899/£899 and is ideal for home offices, general productivity, coding, photo editing and less demanding creative work. Because it launched only in September, a significant Prime Day discount would be particularly attractive.
Mac mini M5 Pro: Best compact professional desktop
Choose the M5 Pro model if you need more CPU and GPU performance, Thunderbolt 5, greater memory bandwidth or more than 32GB of unified memory.
Mac Studio M5 Max: Best professional workstation
The M5 Max Mac Studio offers considerably greater GPU performance, more memory and more connectivity than the Mac mini and is our preferred Studio configuration for most professional users.
iMac: Best all-in-one
The M4 iMac remains the obvious choice if you want an integrated 4.5K display and minimal desk clutter, but its older M4 chip and $1,499/£1,499 starting price mean we’d only recommend it with a substantial discount.
For more advice read:
Should I buy a Mac mini?
Should I buy a Mac Studio?


						

							


Prime Day Mac & MacBook deals to avoid
The cheapest Mac isn’t always the best value. Rather than using Prime Day simply to spend less, use it as an opportunity to get better specifications for the same budget.
When buying a Mac in 2026, try to get as much RAM and storage as you can afford. Most current Macs now start with 16GB of unified memory, although some still have only 256GB of storage. The main exception for memory is the entry-level MacBook Neo, which has 8GB of RAM and a 256GB SSD.
Because Apple silicon Macs can’t have their unified memory or internal storage upgraded later, it’s worth buying enough for your future needs. Memory is particularly important for demanding creative work, development and AI workloads.
For most buyers, prioritizing memory will provide greater long-term benefits than paying extra for a faster processor. Professional users may want 36GB or more, while 64GB or more can be worthwhile for demanding video production, software development and AI workloads.
Don’t buy a MacBook Neo simply because it’s the cheapest Mac: If an M5 Air is only around $200/£200 more, the Air gives you 16GB RAM, better display support and considerably more headroom.
Don’t pay close to full price for an M4 Mac mini: It has now been replaced. Clearance is only attractive if the discount properly reflects that.
Don’t confuse M6 Mac mini with M5 Pro Mac mini: M6 is the mainstream chip; M5 Pro remains much faster for many professional workloads despite the apparently older number. Macworld
Don’t buy a MacBook Pro purely because the discount looks enormous: Apple increased MSRP dramatically in June, so a “$400 off” deal may simply bring it closer to what the machine cost before the increase. Compare the actual selling price with the historic lows in your table.


						

							


Should you buy a MacBook or Mac during Prime Day?
October Prime Day is a good opportunity to buy a Mac, but whether you should take a deal depends on the model.
The M5 MacBook Air is particularly easy to recommend because it is not expected to be replaced until 2027. The new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini are also safe purchases from a product-cycle perspective, although their recent launch means discounts may initially be smaller.
MacBook Pro buyers have a more difficult decision. The current M5 models are powerful machines and a large discount may outweigh the benefit of waiting, but a redesigned MacBook Pro is rumored before the end of 2026.
MacBook Neo buyers should watch the price closely. The previous Prime Day low was $589.99/£549, so a deal near or below those figures would be especially attractive.
We would avoid the iMac because of it’s typically high price and age. 
Finally, remember that Amazon isn’t the only retailer likely to cut prices during Prime Day. Best Buy, Walmart and B&H in the U.S., and retailers including Currys, John Lewis and others in the U.K., may run competing promotions, so compare prices before buying.
Before you buy, keep the following in mind:
Prime membership is required: Many of the best deals are exclusive to Amazon Prime members. If you’re not already subscribed, you might be able to take advantage of Amazon’s 30-day free trial or you could sign up for a month and cancel afterward. As well as getting free two-day shipping, Prime customers also get access to Prime Video and Music. Prime memberships cost $139 / £95 annually, or $14.99 / £8.99 / AU$6.99 every month. 
Other sales: If you miss Prime Day, you’ll have another chance to save during the Black Friday sales in November.
Student Discounts: Students can get discounts at Apple’s Education Store. See: Apple’s U.S. Education Store or Apple’s U.K. Education Store.
Prime Day is available in multiple countries, including Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, Portugal, Singapore, Spain, the U.K., and the U.S.



						

							


Why you can trust Macworld’s recommendations
The MacBooks and Mac desktops picked here are all chosen by our editors, who have decades of experience with Apple devices. We’ve reviewed everything we recommend, and we only highlight deals that are genuinely good value.
The products selected in this article are at the best current price, usually at or near all-time low prices, and we’ve selected what we think is the best configuration for each product type. We know Apple is expensive, so we’ve chosen products at prices we would be willing to pay, so you can trust that our recommendations will steer you in the right direction.

title: iOS 27.2 beta 3 is out now with the new Health app and more
content:
Macworld





Just a couple days after the wide release of iOS 27, Apple has released the first beta of iOS 27.2. That’s not a typo: it’s iOS 27.2, not 27.1. We never saw a 27.1 release, but Apple is beginning beta tests for the 27.2 branch.
This likely has something to do with the iPhone Duo, which is going on sale in October. We know the iPhone Duo will come with iOS 27.1, but we don’t yet know if any other devices will ever get a 27.1 update, or when all the devices will get on the same version together.
Update October 5: The third beta release is out now, shoring up bugs on the way to a wide release later this month.
What’s new in iOS 27.2
As beta testers report new capabilities in this version, we’ll report them here. 
New Health app: The 27.2 beta includes the new Health app, with a totally new redesign and AI-powered health insights.
Siri AI languages: Apple said that Siri AI, which launched supporting only U.S. English, will expand to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
Dual Capture for Group FaceTime: Users can stream their front and rear cameras at the same time during FaceTime calls.
Podcasts Up Next: Up Next has been refreshed with two rows at the top of the Home tab: New Episodes and Continue Playing.
Simple Profiles on iOS/iPadOS/web: The Apple TV feature that lets you use multiple different account profiles now works in the Apple TV app on iOS, iPadOS, and the web.
Multiview in Apple TV: The feature that lets you watch four select sports streams at the same time on Apple TV now works on the Apple TV app on iOS.
iOS 27.2: How to install the public beta
If you want to test the iOS 27 beta releases but are not a registered developer, follow these steps:
Click Sign Up on the Apple Beta page and register with your Apple ID.
Log in to the Beta Software Program.
Click Enroll your iOS device.
Open the Settings app, tap General, then Software Update.
In the Beta Updates section, select the iOS Public Beta.
It may take a few moments after registering for the beta option to appear in Software Update.
iOS 27.2: How to install the developer beta
You’ll need to be registered as an Apple developer, but a free developer account will do. You can get one via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app:
Download the Apple Developer App from the App Store.
Open the app.
Tap on Account.
Sign in using your usual Apple ID.

title: Check out New Balance’s secret tribute to Steve Jobs on the anniversary of his passing
content:
Macworld





On this day 15 years ago, the world lost Steve Jobs after a years-long battle with pancreatic cancer. You’ll read many posts throughout the day about what a great leader and visionary he was, but none will be sweeter or more poignant than the subtle tribute New Balance posted.
If you ever watched one of Steve Jobs’ keynotes, you know his trademark outfit: a black turtleneck, blue jeans, black socks, and a pair of gray New Balance 992s. It’s not flashy or bold, but came to define his brand as much as the products he helped create.
New Balance hasn’t changed the look of the 992 since that time, and it’s still offered in the same “Grey with white” colorway. If you head over there to buy one, you’ll see a photo at the end of the gallery of a person sitting cross-legged wearing a pair. They happen to be wearing blue jeans with black socks and sitting in a black leather chair.

				
					

				
			
Steve Jobs shown wearing the New Balance 992 in Gray (right) next to New Balance’s re-creation of the pose.

Foundry




If you know your Apple history, you’ll recognize that this is the same chair that Steve Jobs famously sat in to conduct the first demo of the original iPad in January 2010. He wanted to show how casual and “intimate” the device was, so he used as if one would while in their home. It would be one of the last times we saw him on stage and one of his most iconic keynotes.
On this day, the image is an especially poignant and a touching tribute to a man who made the shoe famous.

title: The upcoming touchscreen MacBook Pro may be Air-light
content:
Macworld





After years of rumors and speculation, it looks like the first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen is finally almost here. If the latest leaks are to be believed, the device is currently in testing within Apple on macOS 27.2, and should arrive within the next month or so.
This new MacBook Pro won’t just be a current model with a touchscreen. We are expecting a full redesign of Apple’s iconic laptop: visually distinct, with an OLED display, Dynamic Island cutout, and of course a touchscreen. There are design and functionality changes to macOS to support touch, too. We don’t know what it will look like, but the expectation has been that it should seem familiar—everyone knows what a “MacBook” is supposed to look like—but thinner and lighter. In Mark Gurman’s latest Power On newsletter, he lets us know that last point will be especially true.
Gurman says the new OLED and touch MacBook Pro will be “significantly lighter” (emphasis his), with a lot of attention paid to redesigning the interior of the machine, minimizing and consolidating parts to make it lighter and easier to carry. The current 14-inch MacBook Pro is 25 percent heavier than the equivalent MacBook Air, at 3.4 pounds for the 14-inch model (compared to 2.7 pounds for the 13-inch Air). The larger 16-inch model is 4.7 pounds, compared to 3.3 pounds for the 15-inch Air. That’s a 42 percent weight difference.
It would hardly be cause for such emphasis on being dramatically lighter if Apple had achieved only a 10 percent weight reduction, and if it’s 20 percent lighter or more, it’s entering MacBook Air territory. We don’t yet know if the touchscreen MacBook will come in the same sizes or introduce a new sixe at, say 15 inches, but it’s safe to say it will be at least 14 inches. So a “significant” reduction in weight means it will almost certainly clock it at under three pounds, which will definitely be noticeable when carrying it in a bag.

title: iPhone 13 Pro vs. iPhone 18 Pro Buyer's Guide: Is It Worth Upgrading?
content:
Apple released the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max in September 2026, five years after the iPhone 13 Pro and iPhone 13 Pro Max. The 2021 models introduced ProMotion displays, macro photography, a 3x Telephoto camera, and substantially longer battery life than their predecessors. They remain capable phones and support iOS 27, but owners now have five generations of upgrades to consider.


The iPhone 14 Pro brought the Dynamic Island, an Always-On display, a 48-megapixel Main camera, and Emergency SOS via satellite. The iPhone 15 Pro introduced the Action button and USB-C. This year's iPhone 18 Pro adds the A20 Pro chip, a variable-aperture Main camera, a smaller ‌Dynamic Island‌, and further gains in battery life and charging speed. For an iPhone 13 Pro owner, these changes accumulate across nearly every part of the phone.

Is It Worth Upgrading From an iPhone 13 Pro?

For most iPhone 13 Pro and iPhone 13 Pro Max owners ready to replace their phone, the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ is a very worthwhile upgrade. Five years of changes bring noticeable improvements to battery life, charging, outdoor display visibility, photography, and connectivity. The iPhone 13 Pro already has ProMotion and a capable three-camera system, but those strengths do not erase the breadth of the newer model's improvements.

Battery life may be the most immediate benefit, especially for an iPhone 13 Pro whose original battery has aged. Faster wired charging and USB-C also make the newer phone easier to live with, particularly if your other devices already use USB-C.

The camera upgrade is substantial across the whole system. All three rear cameras move from 12 to 48 megapixels, while the variable-aperture Main camera adds creative control and the Telephoto camera extends from 3x to 4x, with an additional optical-quality 8x option. The higher-resolution front camera, autofocus, and Center Stage are useful for group photos and video calls. Video creators gain considerably more through higher frame rates, improved Cinematic mode, external recording, and professional formats.

The A20 Pro and vapor chamber make the strongest performance case for demanding games, long recording sessions, and other sustained work. The ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ also supports ‌Apple Intelligence‌, while the iPhone 13 Pro does not, even though both run ‌iOS 27‌.

The main physical trade-offs are size and weight: both ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ models are taller, thicker, and slightly heavier. Some users may find the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌'s aluminum chassis to be more vulnerable to dents and damage, even though the front and rear glass is stronger. U.S. buyers who rely on a physical SIM must also move to eSIM.

title: Best magnetic power banks and MagSafe portable chargers for iPhone 2026
content:
Macworld





Portable power banks that charge your phone are popular, but wireless battery packs using Apple’s magnetic MagSafe technology offer a simpler and smarter cable-free solution for iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 and Air users.
Phone batteries are prone to run dry just when you’re heading away from a power source, so having a portable charging source is one of today’s necessities. Annoyingly, most power banks require you to carry around a cable, too. Wireless power banks do away with cables but come with their own major limitation—the inefficiency of wireless charging means you need a high-capacity power bank to fully charge a drained iPhone.
MagSafe is a technology that’s compatible with all iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, Air and Duo models, from the mini to the Pro Max, but strangely missing from the 16e model. It allows accessories to clamp magnetically to the back of the iPhone, making the charging connection more efficient. We haven’t yet had an iPhone Duo in for testing with these magnetic power banks, but the new folding iPhone is MagSafe friendly.
We put the best portable chargers through a series of rigorous iPhone recharging tests, and have listed the winners by power, portability and functionality:
Best high-capacity 10k MagSafe power banks
Best small portable 5K magnetic power banks
Best multi-device charging MagSafe power banks 
Best capacity magnetic power bank for you
You should consider size when it comes to a power bank: physical size and battery capacity. The higher the battery capacity, the more recharging power you’ll get from the power bank—but you’ll also be carrying around a larger, heavier item. Lighter, slimmer power banks are easier to pocket even when clamped to your phone. Larger power banks might not fit in your trouser pocket and can slide off easier when pocketed even if clamped magnetically.
10K power banks (with a 10000mAh battery capacity) can charge a phone close to two times over, while 5K (5000mAh) battery packs usually stretch between 60-75%, which is often enough to get you to the next wall-socket powering opportunity. If you are relying on the power bank for long-haul travel or a camping trip, a 10K battery or higher will suit you better. Belkin even offers a mid-range 8K power bank.
Milliamp hours (mAh) is quite a blunt measurement of battery capacity. It’s great for quickly differentiating between power bank sizes but we also list the capacity in the more accurate watt hours (Wh).
Also, look out for power banks that are built using the latest semi-solid-state battery technology that uses less liquid electrolyte than standard litium-ion power banks, making them more durable, longer lasting, and safer.
Wireless power bank charging speed
Wireless charging speeds vary from 7.5W (MagSafe Compatible) to 15W (certified MagSafe and Qi2), all the way to the very fastest wireless charging at 25W (Qi2.2). While it’s not as efficient as using a cable to charge a phone, magnetic wireless charging is a step closer to doing away with cables altogether. Qi2 25W brings wireless charging close to wired speed but only iPhones 16 and later support that speed, and some power banks include a built-in USB-C cable for even faster charging up to 45W. The iPhone Air can manage 20W max on even a 25W charger. See Which wireless tech is best for your iPhone?.
We have listed the speeds at which each portable power bank can be charged itself (Input charger) and charge the iPhone (Output charger). The higher the wattage, the faster the charging should be.
Best high-capacity 10K MagSafe power banks
A 10000mAh (10K) battery is the sweet spot for both power and portability. 5000mAh (5K) power banks reviewed further down are slimmer, lighter and easier to pocket, but generally offer a maximum of 70-80% recharge potential versus a 10K power bank that should be able to recharge an iPhone at least one and a half times over.

The Kuxiu S3 was the first semi-solid-state 25W magnetic wireless power bank to enter the Macworld Lab. A semi-solid state (SSS) power bank is more energy-dense than a traditional liquid electrolyte power bank because its semi-solid electrolyte is less prone to leakage and thermal runaway. SSS is therefore more durable, safer and offers more charge cycles so will last longer.
Indeed, not only does it tick those boxes but its also boasts three other top-end features: a built-in USB-C cable, integrated kickstand, and super-clear digital battery display.
Only the iPhones 16/17/18 support the very fastest wireless tech Qi2 25W, and only the iPhone 15 and later have a USB-C charging port. Older iPhones (from 12 on) can use a 25W charger such as the S3 but are pegged back at 15W—still faster than the 7.5W found on cheaper power banks.
Switch to wired charging via the integrated USB-C cable and you’ll achieve up to 35W so even faster.
The S3 has a 10000mAh (10K) battery capacity and managed to recharge that same iPhone to 177%—so up to 100% then another 77% when it came to a second recharging task. That’s not the top score we’ve had in our 10K power bank tests: the champ so far is the Ugreen MagFlow Air 10K, which scored an unmatched 208%, with the EcoFlow RAPID 10K and Anker MagGo Slim scoring 190% or close—both are reviewed here. But 177% is above average.
The same company offers two other 25W magnetic power banks: the similar S4 reviewed below, and the K1 Ultra (reviewed in our multi-device section below) that has a neat slide-out panel that can charge your Apple Watch or AirPods at the same time as the iPhone.

How we tested
MagSafe charger testing was conducted using an iPhone 13 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro and 16 Pro, subscribed to a 5G network and WiFi, with screen off and all default settings.
Our test is a simple battery recharge shootout. We let our test-unit iPhone Pro (3095mAh battery capacity) drain to just 10% and then set the Battery Pack to work recharging the phone. We then assigned the charger a score of whatever percentage it managed to charge the iPhone to and subtract the 10%; we test each model at least twice.
It’s not a real-world test of day-to-day use where you’ll likely be using your phone for various tasks (of varying battery usage) and in different environmental conditions and network configurations. But it does give us a common score format that we can use to compare different battery-pack models.

				
					

				
			
Why is magnetic wireless better?
The MagSafe connection to Apple’s iPhone is precise enough to make wireless charging more efficient as around 20% of non-magnetic power loss is from poor placement of a phone and the wireless charging pad. Standard Qi wireless charging can lose as much as 50% of the portable battery’s power, but MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging loses ‘just’ 30%. Hot out of the gadget laboratory, the new Qi 2.2 (also known as Qi2 25W) brings even faster 25W wireless charging for the iPhone 16, 17 and 18. 15% will be plenty fast enough for most of us but who doesn’t want the fastest possible charging when your iPhone’s battery icon is in the red?
Why comparing Watt Hours is better than Milliamp Hours
Phone batteries are generally rated in Milliamp Hours (mAh) but this is a measure of electrical charge, while a Watt Hour is equal to one watt of energy consumed for one hour of time.
When comparing battery capacities and how much a power pack will boost a phone’s internal battery, energy is more important than electrical charge.
And mAh ignores a battery voltage, which determines the wattage (power) of a battery.
If the mAh is the same, the higher the voltage, the greater the actual stored power.
For example, Apple’s MagSafe Battery Pack is rated at just 1460mAh but it has a higher voltage potential (7.62V) than the iPhone (3.81V) or other battery packs, meaning that it can provide more power to an iPhone than its mAh suggests; in fact, it is actually 2920mAh.
To go into further depth about this read our feature iPhone battery capacities compared that also lists all iPhones battery life in mAh and Wh.
Anatomy of a magnetic power bank

				
					

				
			
TORRAS




A lot more than a battery goes into the making of a magnetic power bank.
Of course, the battery is the most important component, but the wireless charging coils and magnetic connection are vital for efficient and therefore fast and powerful charging. The transmitter coil transfers power by electromagnetic induction.
The magnets need to be set up to exactly connect the transmitting coils—here on the power bank— to the receiving coils, in this case inside the iPhone.
The example shown above is the Torras MagStall Wireless Power Bank, reviewed in our chart. You can see the various parts, including that power bank’s rotating stand/handle.
Which magnetic wireless tech is right for each iPhone?
iPhone 7 and earlier: Don’t support wireless charging. 
iPhone 8 – iPhone X/XS/XR: Support wireless charging. iPhone 8 and later can charge wirelessly at 7.5W but on a less efficient non-magnetic Qi pad.
iPhone 11 and earlier: Don’t support MagSafe. iPhone 8 and later can charge wirelessly but on a less efficient non-magnetic Qi pad.
iPhone 12 – iPhone 15: Support MagSafe and Qi2. Can wirelessly charge at 7.5W with “MagSafe-Compatible” power banks and chargers, and at 15W with certified MagSafe or Qi2 power banks and chargers.
iPhone 16 – iPhone 18: Support MagSafe, Qi2 and Qi2.2. Can wirelessly charge at 7.5W with “MagSafe-Compatible” power banks and chargers, at 15W with certified MagSafe or Qi2 power banks and chargers, and at 25W with Qi2.2-certified power banks and chargers.
Is charging via a cable faster or safer than magnetic wireless charging?
Charging via a cable is nearly always faster than wireless, even the latest Qi2.2 wireless chargers. Wireless charging is inefficient, losing some of its energy transfer through heat, for example. MagSafe, Qi2, and Qi2.2 magnetic connections dramatically improve efficiency but sticking a cable in is still a faster method, if not as convenient.
Most magnetic wireless power banks include at least one USB-C port, and some even include a port and an integrated cable for ultimate convenience. Models after the iPhone 17 can charge to 50% in 20 minutes or under via a cable and a 45W or higher charger or power bank. But wireless is so simple and cable-free that we don’t mind waiting an extra 15 minutes or so to reach such a charge wirelessly.
Why does my phone occasionally charge slowly or even stop charging?
This phone charging behavior is due to the built-in battery management feature on your iPhone. A phone heats up during charging as power is exchanged between the charger’s coils and the iPhone’s own. The phone actively adjust its charging behavior accordingly. This can slow down or temporarily pause charging to protect battery health and extend its lifespan. This is completely normal. Once the phone cools down, charging will automatically resume as normal.
What is a semi solid state battery?
The material that carries ions back and forth inside a battery is called “electrolyte”. Traditional lithium-ion batteries use a volatile, free-flowing liquid for electrolyte. As their name suggests, solid-state batteries use a solid material such as a ceramic or polymer. But semi-solid-state batteries are more common in today’s new generation of power banks.
A semi-solid-state battery uses a mix of solid particles in a much smaller amount of liquid, making a hybrid thick gel, paste or slurry. By reducing the liquid content to a minimum, semi-solid-state batteries increase stability and durability and significantly lower the risk of leaks, fires, and dangerous thermal runaway.
What about non-wireless power banks?
Wireless charging—especially magnetic wireless charging—is super convenient and does away with the need to carry around messy cables to connect your device to the battery pack.
But wired charging is nearly always faster and not much of an inconvenience if you are not out and about. Over on our sister site Tech Advisor I have reviewed the best power banks that includes standard non-wireless battery packs that might be a decent solution as well as the power banks reviewed above.
Do magnetic power banks work when the iPhone is in a case?
Yes, most quality iPhone cases are compatible with MagSafe having their own magnet ring to ensure a close connection between the power bank’s magnetic charging coils and the iPhone’s own. You can find exactly which are supported in our roundups of the best iPhone 17 cases, best iPhone 16 cases and best iPhone 15 cases.

Which iPad should you buy? 

				
					

				
			
There’s an iPad for everyone.

Foundry




iPad: The budget recommendation
The standard iPad is the best choice if price is your priority. It’s powerful enough for everyday tasks, streaming, schoolwork and casual gaming, but it’s the only current iPad that doesn’t support Apple Intelligence. With a replacement expected in early 2027, we’d look for a substantial Prime Day discount.
iPad mini: Best for portability 
The iPad mini is the best choice if you want maximum portability, but we’d be cautious about buying one this Prime Day. A new model could arrive later in October, with an OLED display among the expected upgrades. Only buy the current model if the discount is good enough to compensate.
iPad Air: Best choice for most buyers
The M4 iPad Air is the best choice for most people and probably the safest Prime Day buy. It offers considerably more performance than the standard iPad without the expense of the Pro, comes in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes, and isn’t expected to be replaced until 2027.
iPad Pro: Best for professionals/creative users
The M5 iPad Pro is aimed at demanding creative and professional users who will benefit from its performance and OLED display. It’s also safe to buy this Prime Day, but most people will get better value from the iPad Air.
For more advice read our guide to the Best iPad.


						

							


Prime Day iPad deals to avoid

				
					

				
			
Dominik Tomaszewski / Foundry




When deciding whether to shop for an iPad deal, we recommend you keep a few things in mind:
If you’re considering an iPad as a laptop replacement, remember to factor in the price of a keyboard. Adding an Apple keyboard case can add hundreds to the cost and, depending on the iPad, push the total close to or above the price of a MacBook. The arrival of the lower-cost MacBook Neo makes that comparison even more important.
Be particularly cautious about iPad mini deals. The current A17 Pro model could be replaced as soon as later in October, with an OLED display among the expected upgrades. Unless the Prime Day discount is substantial, you may be better off waiting.
The iPad (A16) is currently the only tablet in Apple’s active lineup that does not support Apple Intelligence. A replacement is expected in early 2027, so avoid paying close to Apple’s full price. A substantial discount, however, can still make the current model a good-value choice.
Deals on older or refurbished iPads can be tempting, but check software support before buying. iPadOS 27 drops support for several older models, so make sure the iPad you’re considering can run the current operating system.
Avoid paying extra for a Cellular model unless you truly need it. Cellular versions cost significantly more and may also require a monthly data plan. If you usually carry an iPhone, Personal Hotspot is often a cheaper alternative.
Casual users should also think twice before jumping on an iPad Pro (M5) deal. Unless you need its OLED display or additional performance for demanding creative and professional workflows, the M4 iPad Air offers better value for most people.
Likewise, don’t pay extra for the iPad Pro’s nano-texture glass unless you regularly work in bright or uncontrolled lighting.


						

							


Should you buy an iPad during Prime Day?
October Prime Day is one of the better times of the year to buy an iPad, particularly after Apple raised iPad prices substantially in June. Amazon’s October sale often comes close to Black Friday pricing, so a good deal could offset much of Apple’s price increase. 
The model you choose matters, though. The M4 iPad Air and M5 iPad Pro are relatively safe buys because neither is expected to be replaced until 2027. The A16 iPad can also be worth buying at a substantial discount, although it is the only current iPad without Apple Intelligence. We’d be much more cautious about the iPad mini, as a new model could arrive soon after Prime Day.
There are a few other things to consider before making a purchase:
Prime membership is required: Many of the best deals are exclusive to Amazon Prime members. If you’re not already subscribed, you might be able to take advantage of Amazon’s 30-day free trial or you could sign up for a month and cancel afterward. As well as getting free two-day shipping, Prime customers also get access to Prime Video and Music. Prime memberships cost $139 / £95 annually, or $14.99 / £8.99 / AU$6.99 every month. 
Other sales: If you miss Prime Day, you’ll have another chance to save during the Black Friday sales in November which historically brings some of the lowest iPad prices of the year.
Student Discounts: Students can save significantly through the Apple Education Store. For example, students can save $50/£50 on the iPad Air and $100/£100 on the iPad Pro when shopping at Apple’s U.S. Education Store or Apple’s U.K. Education Store.
Compare Prices: Amazon isn’t always the cheapest option. Retailers such as Walmart and Best Buy frequently run competing promotions around the time of Prime Day, so it’s worth comparing prices before buying.
Prime Day is available in multiple countries, including Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, Portugal, Singapore, Spain, the U.K., and the U.S.


						

							


Why you can trust Macworld’s recommendations
The Prime Day iPad deals picked here are all chosen by our editors, who have decades of experience with Apple devices. We’ve reviewed everything we recommend, and we won’t tell you to buy something that’s not an actual deal. We track current prices against previous lows and only highlight discounts we think are worth considering. During Prime Day, we continually update this page as better deals appear, selecting the configurations that offer the best value for each product type. Apple products are expensive, so we focus on prices we’d be willing to pay ourselves—and deals we believe will genuinely save you money.


						

							




Prime Day 2026: More outstanding Apple deals
Throughout the Prime Day sale, we constantly check Amazon’s listings to find the best deals. We’ve tested all of the models we recommend here and only select the very best deals—so if you see an iPad listed here, you’ll know it’s at or near its all-time low price. And it’s not just iPads.

title: Mac Users Reclaim 12GB+ of Storage With Apple Intelligence Removal Tool
content:
A new open-source tool is making waves in the Mac community by helping users reclaim valuable storage space taken up by Apple's AI models. Called "RemoveMacAI," the command line tool disables Apple Intelligence on macOS 27, removes its downloaded models, and prevents them from being downloaded again.


In macOS 27, Apple removed the toggle to disable Apple Intelligence wholesale, and simply disabling individual features doesn't remove the models from your Mac's drive. As explained by the developer, RemoveMacAI gets around this by using a configuration profile to switch off Apple's own asset management service and remove the models. 

It then configures the system so attempts to download the removed models are redirected to a closed local port, preventing them from immediately coming back. And it does all this without disabling System Integrity Protection (SIP) or manually deleting files from protected system locations, unlike some older tools have.

The tool can free up roughly 12GB of space depending on which models are present on your Mac. That said, some users are reporting cases of Apple Intelligence models having taken up a lot more space, which they've now reclaimed. 

With the Apple models gone, you lose all Siri-related AI features, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, ChatGPT integration, summaries, smart replies, inline predictions, Photos Clean Up, Spatial Photos, and Xcode predictive completion. Even so, plenty of users appear happy to make the sacrifice to free up space, especially on non-upgradeable Macs with 256GB of storage. The profile reportedly persists across updates. And if you're wondering, dictation still works. There's also a revert command to restore everything AI-related.

GitHub stars since its release last week, and there's lots of discussion on Reddit and Hacker News about the need for such a tool. Just be aware that MacRumors isn't endorsing RemoveMacAI, and anyone using it does so at their own risk.

title: Apple’s next big thing may be even riskier than the iPhone Duo
content:
Macworld





This time next week, the Apple world could look very different. We may have received (and doubtless be obsessing over the artwork and tagline of) invitations to an event on October 13, when reputable sources say the company will unveil its next big thing. Or, based on other clues, namely the arrival in Apple retail stores of mysterious boxes to be opened on October 8, the information may have already emerged.
Whether it appears this Thursday or next Tuesday, and whether it’s announced via a big press event or a humble press release, Apple’s next big thing will almost certainly be its first bona fide smart-home product: a hub, made up of a vaguely HomePod-like speaker topped by a vaguely iPad-like screen. We in the media have taken to calling it the HomePad, but if the recent launches of the MacBook Neo and iPhone Duo are anything to go by, Apple will probably call it something short and cute and random, ending with an O. The HomePod Echo, perhaps. Or perhaps not.
The real issue with the HomePad is not its name, but its niche. Potential customers will ask every marketing manager’s most feared question: What is it for? If Apple hasn’t come up with an answer in the multiple years the product has been in development, it’s unlikely something will spring to mind in the next eight days. But one way or another an answer will be needed.
As I hinted with my silly Echo joke, this isn’t an unprecedented concept or a new market. Amazon’s closest rival is probably the Echo Show 8 (the Show 5 is closer in screen size, but has a different design), while Google has the Nest Hub, and both sit in the space Apple will be looking to dominate. The presence of these incumbents might seem like a good omen for the company, which loves to wait until a market is established before taking a swing with the definitive product. But as with the foldable iPhone Duo, there are two problems: First, while tech fans in general are intimately familiar with the concept, Apple’s own fans are not. And second, Apple’s version is likely to be more expensive.
The original HomePod may be an illustrative comparison here. Apple was expected to go after the smart speaker market, but ended up leaning far more on the second word than the first. The HomePod is sort of smart, but it’s really just a nice, decent-quality speaker you can command (some of the time…) using your voice. And so Apple didn’t end up displacing products like the Echo and the Nest because the HomePod couldn’t do what they do and didn’t really try, while overachieving in other areas and costing more. And Apple customers, unless they were bold enough to become platform-agnostic, remained outside that bubble.
Siri is a lot smarter now than it was then (not that you’d know it from the performance of legacy HomePod models, unfortunately), so the chances are that Apple will try to do the smart-home concept properly this time. The HomePad will run Siri AI, and thus be able to field questions, surface information from your messages and email inbox, and use natural language. It will have excellent capabilities. But again, the question is what we will use these capabilities for. Where will it sit? What functions will it perform? Speaking personally, I’m not sure how it would fit in my life. So the product’s introduction will need to do a great deal of imaginative heavy lifting.
Let’s say the HomePad sits in the kitchen. Useful for recipes, perhaps, although it’s important to remember that it will only have a 6-inch screen and thus won’t match an iPad for legibility. Or it might sit in the living room and act as the hub for smart-home controls. But what proportion of Apple fans actually use HomeKit smart lights, smart door locks, and a smart thermostat so much that they need a dedicated device? A relatively small one, I’d guess, and those that do will be accustomed to controlling them via automations or manual control on an iPhone. Or even voice controls via a HomePod.
At least with the iPhone Duo, Apple had some user experience to lean on. It is, after all, still a phone, albeit one that’s a little smaller than we’re used to, with the ability to offer a bigger screen than we’re used to. But customers get what it’s offering. It’s a phone, only conceptually better. (And pragmatically, in some ways, rather worse.) You don’t need to make such an imaginative leap of faith.
But the HomePad doesn’t really have a precedent in Apple’s walled garden. It’s a HomePod with a screen. But having a screen (and offering voice control which actually works) massively expands its capabilities in one area, while cutting the speaker down to a tiny hemisphere, as is predicted, slashes them in another. What we end up with isn’t remotely like a HomePod in form or function. It’s something new. And new is scary.
So Apple’s crack marketing team has another challenge on their hands. If you thought the iPhone Duo was an exciting, radical, risky product, wait for the HomePad.
Or whatever they end up calling it. Something short and cute and random. Ending with an O.

				
					

				
			
Foundry
