title: New HomePod rumors: HomePod mini 2, HomePad and touchscreen HomePod
content:
Macworld





Apple’s HomePod lineup could be about to undergo its biggest expansion since the original HomePod launched. Apple is reportedly preparing a new HomePod mini and smart home display for October 13, with another full-size HomePod expected further down the line, as it builds a new generation of home products around Siri AI.
For much of 2025 and 2026, Apple’s revamped Siri was the thing holding those products back. That’s no longer the case: Siri AI has now arrived with Apple’s OS 27 updates, removing one of the biggest obstacles to launching the new hardware. The HomePod mini 2 appears to be particularly close, with Apple code discovered in September 2026 revealing images of the unreleased speaker and its five colors, while Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in July that a new HomePod mini, Apple TV and smart home display are among Apple’s upcoming home products.
The naming is less straightforward. “HomePad,” “Smart Home Hub,” “Personal Hub” and “HomePod Touch” are all placeholder names being used for different rumored products or concepts, rather than confirmed Apple names. In this article, we’re using “HomePad,” “Smart Home Hub” and “Personal Hub” for the standalone smart display reportedly being developed for smart-home controls, Siri AI and video calls, while “HomePod Touch” refers specifically to reports about a HomePod-style speaker with an integrated touchscreen.
There may ultimately be some overlap between these products, and some of the rumored concepts could be combined, renamed or never released at all. Below, we separate what is currently known about each device and when it is likely to arrive.







What are the new HomePod products?
Apple is reportedly developing several new HomePod and smart-home products. The names below aren’t official Apple names; where necessary, we’re using placeholder names to distinguish between the different rumored devices.


Placeholder nameWhat is it When 

HomePod mini 2New HomePod mini with the same basic design, new colors, faster processor and Siri AI support.October 13, 2026 (rumored)
HomePad/Smart Home Hub6-inch smart display with Siri AI, Home controls, apps and camera; tabletop and wall-mounted versions expected.October 13, 2026 (rumored)
HomePod 3Next-generation full-size HomePod with faster hardware and Siri AI supportIn development, but reportedly not imminent
HomePod TouchHomePod with a built-in 6-inch touchscreen.Uncertain; no firm launch window
Robotic home screen Display mounted on a robotic arm 2027 or beyond
Security cameraApple-designed home security cameraTiming uncertain

 






Why have Apple’s new Home products taken so long?
Apple’s next generation of smart-home products appears to have been delayed largely because of Siri. The company was developing a much more capable version of Siri for Apple Intelligence, while the processors inside the current HomePod mini and second-generation HomePod weren’t designed to run Apple’s latest AI features.
That created a problem for new HomePod hardware. Apple was reportedly preparing products such as a new HomePod mini and smart home display around the capabilities of the redesigned assistant, but Siri’s delayed development meant the hardware couldn’t launch as originally expected.
That situation has now changed. Siri AI arrived with Apple’s OS 27 updates in September 2026, removing one of the main dependencies that had been holding back Apple’s smart-home plans. Recent reports suggest the HomePod mini 2 and Apple’s smart home display are among the products closest to release.
The full-size HomePod appears to be on a different timetable, however. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in September that Apple is testing a new full-size HomePod with Siri AI support, but said it “doesn’t appear to be imminent.” That means we no longer expect the HomePod 3 to necessarily arrive alongside the HomePod mini 2.








HomePod mini 2 rumors
We’ll start off with the rumors about the HomePod mini 2. The HomePod mini is Apple’s smaller, more affordable smart speaker. The new model is expected to offer a new red color option, major processor upgrade and improved connectivity.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




When is the HomePod mini 2 expected to launch?
October 13, 2026
Apple introduced the original HomePod mini in November 2020, so it is now nearly six years old and overdue for an update.
Rumours of a successor have circulated for more than a year. In January 2025, reports suggested a launch toward the end of 2025, and Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman subsequently said that new HomePod mini and Apple TV models were expected in fall 2025. Those products never materialised.
Attention then shifted to spring 2026, with reports suggesting Apple’s new smart home devices would launch alongside its redesigned Siri. However, that timetable also slipped as Apple continued work on its AI-powered assistant.
The latest reports now point to an October 13, 2026 launch. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has several smart home products that are nearly ready but is waiting for the redesigned Siri to ship with the OS 27 updates before introducing new hardware.
If those plans remain on schedule, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to launch alongside Apple’s broader refresh of its smart home lineup this fall, with most reports pointing to October.
What changes are coming to the HomePod mini 2?
Black, blue, green, pink, and white color finishes.
The current HomePod mini is available in Midnight, White, Blue, Yellow and Orange. In September, MacRumors spotted Apple code that revealed five colors for the new model: black, blue, green, pink, and white.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in September 2025, that Apple has tested additional colors for the next-generation model, including red, but it appears that red didn’t make the final cut. 
Otherwise, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to retain the same compact, spherical design as the current model, with no major external changes rumored. Instead, Apple is reportedly focusing on upgraded internal hardware, including an S9 or newer chip capable of supporting Apple’s latest Siri AI features.
Other changes coming to HomePod mini 2
Beyond the color changes revealed in Apple code, the main expected hardware upgrade is a newer processor capable of supporting Siri AI. Reports also point to newer Apple networking and Ultra Wideband hardware, along with possible audio improvements.
Siri AI support: A newer processor should allow the HomePod mini 2 to support Apple’s latest Siri AI features, something the current S5-based model wasn’t designed for.
Improved connectivity: Reports have pointed to Apple’s newer in-house networking hardware, Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip.
Audio improvements: Apple is expected to upgrade the speaker’s audio hardware and processing.
Other internal upgrades: Further hardware refinements are possible.






HomePad/Smart Home Hub rumors
Possible launch: October 13, 2026, according to Bloomberg
Strategy: A new smart-home display category for Apple
HomePad release date 
Apple’s first smart home display could launch on October 13, 2026. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple plans to introduce its new smart-home products on that date, with the long-rumored home hub expected to be the centerpiece of the launch. 
There are signs that Apple could make an announcement even earlier. Confidential retail-display boxes have arrived in Apple Stores, reportedly marked for opening on October 8. This suggests that a product launch is imminent, although it is unclear what the materials relate to. The iPhone Duo goes on sale October 23, so October 8 would appear too early to be connected to that.
Apple has not confirmed the date, and Gurman’s report does not say whether the products will be unveiled at an event or announced through Apple’s website. 
The product had originally been expected earlier in 2026, but its launch was repeatedly pushed back while Apple completed the Siri AI technology that arrived with its September OS 27 updates. Gurman previously reported that the hardware had been ready for some time, with Siri the main reason for the delay.
Apple’s own software has also provided evidence that the product is approaching launch. References discovered in macOS identify J490/HomeAccessory17,1 and J491/HomeAccessory17,2, which are believed to correspond to the tabletop and wall-mounted versions of Apple’s smart home hub.
Earlier reports had only narrowed the launch window to 2026, while a March post from leaker Kosutami hinted at a fall release. Those reports have now been superseded by Gurman’s more specific October 13 timeframe.
What is the HomePad?
The HomePad – also referred to as Apple’s Smart Home Hub or home display – is expected to be a compact 6-inch smart display designed to act as a central interface for the home. It would combine Siri AI, smart-home controls, FaceTime, media playback and Apple services in a device intended to remain plugged in on a countertop, desk, bedside table or wall.
The latest reports suggest that it will be considerably smaller than many earlier concept images implied. A six-inch square display would measure only about 4.25 inches across each side, making it much more of a close-up personal device than an iPad-sized family display. It is likely to be more “desk scale” than “room scale.” 
Apple’s new Siri AI is expected to be central to the HomePad experience. Its delayed development appears to have been one of the main reasons the hardware did not launch earlier.

				
					

				
			
Foundry / ChatGPT




HomePad design, features and specs
Reported features include:
6-inch display: The latest Bloomberg report points to a six-inch display with rounded corners, making the device considerably smaller than many earlier renders suggested.
iMac G4-style tabletop design: The standard model is reportedly mounted above a circular metal speaker base on a polished metal arm, with a design said to be reminiscent of the classic iMac G4. 
Colors: Leaker itspdfu has suggested Rose Pink, Silver, Space Gray and Starlight based on Photo Face setup assets.
Tilting display: The screen is reportedly designed to tilt forward and backward manually.
Wall-mounted version: A second model is reportedly designed to mount on a wall, with a thin square base containing the speakers and microphones.
No battery: The device is expected to remain plugged in, reportedly using USB-C for power.
Siri AI: Apple’s new Siri technology is expected to be central to the device.
Smart-home controls: It should act as a central interface for Home accessories.
FaceTime and communication: A front-facing camera is expected to support FaceTime calls.
User recognition: The device is reportedly designed to recognize household members by face and voice, then display that person’s own calendar, reminders, notes and other information.
Visitor mode: Reports suggest it will be able to hide personal information when guests are using the device.
iPhone authentication: A nearby iPhone may be used for stronger authentication when required.
Other software clues and reports suggest the device could also offer:
Apple apps and services: Reports specifically mention Calendar, Messages, Photos, FaceTime, Notes, Reminders, Music, Podcasts and smart-home controls.
Entertainment: The device is also expected to function as an entertainment hub for streaming music and video, as well as making FaceTime calls via a built-in camera.
New home-focused software: The device is reportedly running a new interface combining elements of Apple Watch, Apple TV and iPhone/iPad software, including widgets, clock faces and photo displays rather than simply running iPadOS. 
No App Store expected at launch: Current reports do not mention an App Store, suggesting the HomePad may initially operate more like a dedicated smart-home appliance than a general-purpose iPad.
Other clues about HomePad software:
Kitchen integration: A new “CookingKit” framework and expanded food sections in Apple News indicate that kitchen assistance, such as searching for recipes by ingredient, could be a primary selling point.
Advanced home control: Code found in the iOS 26 Home app describes an “Adaptive Temperature” feature, which could allow the HomePad to offer more granular control over smart thermostats, including energy-saving optimizations based on local electricity rates.






HomePod 3 rumors
The larger HomePod is more expensive than the HomePod mini, delivering richer, louder audio with deeper bass and spatial audio. The next generation is expected to get a processor upgrade, improved connectivity and better sound.

				
					

				
			
Michael Brown/Foundry




When is the HomePod 3 expected to launch?
Release date: Unknown; not expected imminently
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in September 2026 that Apple was testing a new full-size HomePod with Siri AI support, but that the release did not appear to be imminent.
What changes are coming to the HomePod 3?
Unlike the HomePod mini 2, there are relatively few leaks about hardware upgrades coming to the full-size HomePod. However, it’s expected to receive the same core internal upgrades needed to support Apple’s AI ambitions.
Expected improvements include: 
More powerful chip: The current HomePod uses the S7 chip from the Apple Watch Series 7. A next-generation model is expected to adopt a significantly faster Apple silicon chip, potentially the S9 or newer, to support Apple Intelligence features.
Siri AI support: The upgraded hardware should allow the HomePod to run Apple’s new Siri AI features that aren’t supported by the current S7-based model.
Improved Connectivity: Rumours point to Apple’s in-house networking chip, together with Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip for improved performance and smart home integration.
Audio Enhancements: Apple is also expected to refine the speaker system with upgraded drivers and audio processing.
In September, a post by itspdfu, who has a history of posting leaks online, said that audioOS27, the operating system for HomePod devices, supports Siri AI. The same source claimed that a future HomePod could also include new animations for its top display.
Beyond these internal upgrades, some reports suggest Apple is experimenting with a HomePod featuring a built-in display. That device is expected to be a separate product rather than a standard HomePod 3, and we cover those rumours in the next section.






HomePod with touchscreen (HomePod Touch) rumors
Apple has been rumored to be working on a HomePod with a screen for years, although exactly what form that product will take remains unclear. Older reports have described a HomePod-style speaker with an integrated touchscreen, sometimes referred to unofficially as a “HomePod Touch.”
There is considerable uncertainty here because some older reports about a “HomePod with a display” may describe the same product that more recent reports characterize as Apple’s HomePad or smart home hub. We are treating the HomePod Touch separately here only where reports specifically describe a HomePod-style speaker with an integrated screen.
That is a little more internally consistent and makes the distinction from the HomePad clear without implying that the HomePod Touch is definitely a separate product.





				
					

				
			
Foundry and Apple




When could the touchscreen HomePod launch?
Possible launch: Unknown
Apple has been working on redesigning the HomePod to include a display for some time. Back in March 2023, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo claimed Apple would “unveil a redesigned HomePod featuring a 7-inch panel.” Kuo initially expected this product to arrive in the first half of 2024, but that timeline slipped. In December 2024, he reported further delays had pushed the launch to after WWDC 2025, citing software development challenges. Then, in March 2025, Kuo suggested the device had been delayed again, due to Apple Intelligence setbacks.
Those predictions have all passed without a product appearing. Siri AI has since arrived, but there is currently no firm report giving this touchscreen HomePod a new launch date. It is therefore possible that earlier reports referred to a product that has evolved, been delayed further, or overlaps with Apple’s separately reported HomePad project.

				
					

				
			
HomePod with display incoming?

Foundry




What could the touchscreen HomePod be like?
Display size: 6 and 7-inch touchscreens.
Software: Custom touchscreen operating system running apps like Weather, Calendar, Photos, HomeKit as well as Apple Music
One of the biggest limitations of today’s HomePod is that almost every interaction relies on Siri. A built-in display would provide a more direct way to control music, manage smart home devices and access information, putting Apple’s device in direct competition with the Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub.
According to current rumours, Apple’s display-equipped HomePod will feature a 6-7-inch touchscreen and run a touch-optimised version of homeOS, allowing it to function as both a smart speaker and a smart home hub. Unlike existing HomePods, it is expected to use a far more powerful A-series chip – possibly an A18 or similar – to support Apple’s redesigned AI-powered Siri and the more demanding graphical interface.
Rumoured features:
Large touchscreen: A 6-7-inch display for controlling smart home devices, viewing photos, checking the weather, following recipes and interacting with apps.
Powerful Apple silicon: An A-series chip is expected to replace the S-series processor used in current HomePods, providing the performance needed for Apple Intelligence and the touchscreen interface.
Smart-home controls: A touchscreen HomePod would logically offer easier access to Home controls, although reports about apps and a dedicated smart-home interface may refer instead to Apple’s separate HomePad project
Improved connectivity: Apple’s in-house networking chip, Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip are all rumoured.
FaceTime camera: Reports suggest Apple may include a built-in camera for FaceTime and other video-based features. These could instead relate to Apple’s separate HomePad project.
Possible modular design: Some less-established reports have suggested that a display could dock with a speaker base. This has not been corroborated by the more recent reports describing Apple’s HomePad.
If accurate, this would represent Apple’s biggest expansion of the HomePod lineup since its debut, transforming it from a voice-first speaker into a full smart home controller.

				
					

				
			Amazon Echo Show beside the HomePod mini, 
Ben Patterson/Foundry




Apple robotic home display rumors
Possible launch: 2027 or later
Strategy: A premium smart-home device with a movable display
Apple is also developing a much more ambitious smart-home device that shouldn’t be confused with the HomePad expected first (see above).
As far back as April 2021, Mark Gurman described a high-end device combining a HomePod speaker, a touchscreen, and a camera mounted on a robotic arm that could follow the user around the room during video calls. Gurman has made various references to this over the years.
The device, previously identified as J595, is reportedly an iPad-like display attached to a motorized robotic arm. The arm would allow the screen to move and reposition itself, potentially following a person around the room during FaceTime calls or turning toward whoever is speaking.
Bloomberg has described it as a higher-end smart-home command center that could combine videoconferencing, home controls and security functions. Unlike the stationary HomePad, this appears to be a significantly more complex—and probably more expensive—product. Earlier reports have suggested a price that could reach around $1,000.
The robotic display is also believed to be further away than the HomePad. Previous reports placed it in late 2026 or 2027 at the earliest, and Apple’s more recent software leaks have focused on the J490 and J491 stationary home hubs rather than J595.
What could the robotic display do?
Reported capabilities include:
A large display mounted on a motorized arm.
Automatically turning toward the person using it.
FaceTime and other video calling.
Siri AI and smart-home controls.
Cameras and gesture recognition
Reports suggest cameras could support FaceTime, security monitoring and potentially recognition of users or gestures. Apple has also previously filed patents describing HomePod-related gesture controls, although patents do not necessarily indicate features destined for a shipping product.






What chips will power the new HomePods?
The biggest limitation of today’s HomePods isn’t their speakers – it’s their processors. The HomePod mini still uses the Apple Watch S5 chip introduced in 2019, while the second-generation HomePod runs on the newer, but still relatively modest, S7 chip from the Apple Watch Series 7.
Those chips are powerful enough for music playback, Home controls and existing Siri functions, but they were not designed to run the new Siri AI capabilities introduced with Apple’s OS 27 generation.
That hardware gap helps explain why Apple is expected to introduce new HomePod hardware rather than bringing the full Siri AI experience to the existing models.
HomePod mini 2 & HomePod 3
Gurman has said the main hardware change he has specifically reported for the new HomePods is a faster chip, although he has not identified which processor Apple will use.
HomePod with a screen
The display-equipped HomePod is expected to require substantially more processing power than Apple’s existing smart speakers. Because it will reportedly run a touch-based operating system alongside Apple Intelligence, most analysts expect it to use an A-series processor, with an A17 Pro or A18 among the leading predictions. Apple has not confirmed the chip, and these reports remain speculative.
Whatever processors Apple ultimately chooses, the goal appears to be the same across the entire HomePod range: replacing ageing Apple Watch chips with modern Apple silicon capable of delivering the full Apple Intelligence experience.






New HomePod Prices
The prices for the HomePods increased in June 2026:
HomePod: $349/£349 (was $299/£299)
HomePod mini: $129/£129 (was $99/£99)
Apple raised HomePod prices in June 2026, so we wouldn’t expect the new models to return automatically to the previous $99/$299 price points.
However, a HomePod with a built-in screen could command a higher price. It may launch as a separate product altogether, potentially starting around $399/£399, or higher, depending on features.






Buying advice: Should you wait or buy a HomePod now? 
Wait if: You are considering a HomePod mini. A replacement now appears close, with reports pointing to fall 2026 and Apple code already revealing the unreleased model.
Buy now if: You need a HomePod immediately and find a worthwhile discount. The current HomePod and HomePod mini still work well as speakers and smart-home hubs, but their older processors mean they aren’t designed for Apple’s newer Siri AI capabilities.
If you want a screen: Wait. Apple’s first dedicated home display appears much closer than the more speculative touchscreen HomePod.






What is on Apple’s Smart Home Roadmap
September 2026: Apple’s OS 27 generation introduced its new Siri AI capabilities, removing one of the major software dependencies that had reportedly delayed Apple’s new home hardware.
Fall 2026: The HomePod mini 2 is expected, with October currently the leading possibility.
Fall 2026: Apple’s HomePad/smart home display could also launch, although its timing is less certain.
Beyond 2026: A new full-size HomePod is being tested, but Bloomberg reports that it does not appear imminent.
2027 or later: Apple’s more ambitious robotic home display could follow.
Timing unknown: Apple is also reportedly developing home-security camera hardware.

title: Apple’s home hub isn’t what you think it is
content:
Macworld





Apple may be less than two weeks away from releasing an all-new product in a new device category: a smart home hub. The device is said to be the start of a big push into the smart home category, which Apple has really only dabbled with so far. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says Apple is finally set to announce it on October 13, after years of waiting for the new Siri AI to arrive, which will play a central role in the new device.
According to the most reliable leaks and rumors, this is what we know of the device’s design and operation:
It will have a square aspect ratio with rounded corners and a 6-inch (diagonal) display.
It won’t have a battery, relying instead on USB-C for power.
It will have a metal, round base with perforated holes for the speakers and microphones.
It will attach to the countertop base via a polished metal arm, “reminiscent” of the classic iMac G4.
It will have a single front-facing FaceTime camera.
Additionally, the device is said to run on a new operating system that combines the “StandBy” type widgets and display of the iPhone, screens and faces like the Apple Watch, and some of the media capabilities of Apple TV. A secondary version that mounts to a wall is said to be in the works, too.
There will be clocks and photo displays, of course, but the device will primarily control smart home devices via a Home app of sorts, and include Apple Music, Calendar, Podcasts, Messages, FaceTime, News, Notes, and Reminders. There is no reported mention of an App Store, so it appears as though this is an accessory rather than a standalone platform.
A core feature is said to be user recognition. Since this is meant to be stationary in your home and not portable, it has to work for all the people in your house. So it recognizes people via their face and voice, and then customizes the display to their own preferences, showing their own data and accessing their own calendar, notes, reminders, and so on. 
But if you’re expecting an iPad-like experience, think again.
A tiny 6-inch display
Apple sites like ours have been reporting on this so-called HomePad for ages. Apple has had it more or less ready to go for a long time, but it will rely on Siri for use, and Siri only just got its big brain transplant, so the home hub has sat on the back burner. We’ve largely envisioned a larger device that can act as a centerpiece of a room, something like an iPad or a small iMac.
But based on the latest rumors, most of the renders and mock-ups you see online have the scale all wrong, and it may have given you the wrong impression of its size.

				
					

				
			Macrumors
Over at MacRumors, you will have seen the above mockup, with the square screen over what looks a lot like an iMac G4 base. There’s no scale present, so of course it could be tiny, but the size of the text and number of tiles on the screen makes it seem like it’s hovering over a big iMac G4-like base. That makes the display appear closer to 8-10 inches on a side, or maybe 12 inches diagonal.

				
					

				
			9to5Mac
Mockups like this one from 9to5Mac are common, too, with a display (in this case not square) on top of a standard HomePod. The regular HomePod is 5.6 inches wide. So this mockup shows a screen at least 7 inches wide, or 8.75 inches diagonal.
A square display with a diagonal measurement of 6 inches is only 4.25 inches on each side. That’s only about 1.5 times as wide as an iPhone 18 Pro. Amazon’s Echo Show and Google Nest Hub are both larger than six inches and have widescreen displays. The HomePad will seem minuscule by comparison.

				
					

				
			
This ChatGPT-generated image of Apple’s upcoming smart home hub gives an idea of how small it might be, according to rumors.

Foundry / ChatGPT




Our shameless AI-generated mockup shows what that would look like to scale. Perhaps the base will be a HomePod mini-like half-dome. Maybe it will be more of fat, round coaster. But a rounded-square 6-inch display is really rather small—for comparison, a regular iPhone is more than 30 percent taller!
This scale makes some sense, especially if Apple is trying to make this an affordable device where you buy several and scatter them around the house. But it also speaks to how Apple intends its customers to use it.
How might you use it?
A square display that is only six inches diagonal makes this device much more like an iPhone on a stick than an iPad, or even an iPad mini. That really limits its usefulness for large rooms. This isn’t the kind of thing you can hope to read while standing 10 feet away or hold FaceTime calls from across your living room. It’s more personal than that.
The ability to use it in the kitchen is going to depend very much on the size of your kitchen and where you put it. With enlarged text, you might be able to read a recipe from five or six feet away, but not much more than that. FaceTime calls are really only going to feel good when you’re right up near it. On the other hand, this becomes the perfect little gadget to sit on your bedside table, working as a smart alarm clock, noise machine, and podcast speaker.
While it doesn’t really make sense as an “across the living room” device, it would fit nicely on the end table next to your couch. It seems to be something that’s a little easier to ignore when you’re not using it, rather than a centerpiece. More like a HomePod mini than an iMac in that way.
It also means the base will be of limited size, and that puts limits on the sound volume and quality. Don’t expect the room-filling sound of the big HomePod, but rather something best for podcasts, audiobooks, or music at a modest volume and close distance.
Of course, we won’t really know what it looks like or how big it is until Apple announces it. The rumors about its design have been remarkably consistent over the last couple of years, but we don’t have leaked CAD drawings or parts from parts suppliers or anything like that to go from to know the scale. If the rumors are accurate, you should expect this home hub to be something “desk scale” rather than “room scale.”

title: Microsoft 365 Work Accounts May Stop Syncing in Apple Mail
content:
From October 1, 2026, Microsoft began disabling Exchange Web Services (EWS) by default in Exchange Online, which will cut off the protocol that Apple's Mail and Calendar apps on Mac still rely on to sync Microsoft 365 work accounts.


The cutoff has been on the cards for a fairly long time, as Microsoft stopped adding new features to EWS back in 2018, while in 2023 it announced that it would start disabling the protocol in Exchange Online from October 2026.

recently updated post from June, Microsoft described the change as a "phased rollout," so some Mac users could lose access sooner than others.

It's still possible for IT administrators to restore access. However, Microsoft plans to shut down EWS in Exchange Online permanently on April 1, 2027, and no extensions are currently planned.

support document, the company says it is "actively working with Microsoft" to move Mail, Calendar, Contacts, Notes, and Reminders apps on Mac to the newer Microsoft Graph API in a future macOS 27 update.

Except, that update hasn't arrived yet. Apple skipped macOS 27.1 betas entirely, while release notes for the macOS 27.2 betas have yet to make any mention of Graph support.

Meanwhile, affected organizations can just keep EWS running or move Mac users to a Graph-compatible client, such as Microsoft's Outlook app.

Note that the change will only affect Microsoft's cloud-hosted email server. In other words, companies that run their own Exchange servers aren't affected. Neither will iPhone and iPad be impacted, since they use Exchange ActiveSync rather than EWS.

(Thanks, Jonathan!)

title: When is Apple’s next event? Dates, rumors, and what to expect
content:
Macworld





Apple’s September event may not have been Apple’s final event of 2026 – another launch could be coming on October 13.
Apple typically has four main event windows each year: a spring event, WWDC in June, the iPhone event in September, and sometimes a further event in October. The company rarely confirms dates far in advance, and there’s no guarantee it will hold an event in every window. That leaves Apple fans – and anyone considering a new Apple device – wondering when the next event will happen and what might be announced.
Fortunately, Apple’s annual schedule is fairly predictable, while reliable rumours often provide additional clues about what’s coming. That means we can make informed estimates about the timing of future keynotes and the products most likely to appear.
Here’s everything we know about the event Apple could hold later in 2026 and beyond.


When is Apple’s next event?
Next rumored product launch: October 13, 2026. An event remains unconfirmed.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has claimed on X that Apple will launch its “next big thing” on October 13, referring to new smart-home products. 
However, there are signs that Apple could make an announcement even earlier. Confidential retail-display boxes reportedly marked for opening on October 8 suggest that new products could be imminent, although it is unclear what the materials relate to. October 8 would appear too early for them to be connected to the iPhone Duo, which goes on sale October 23.
Apple has not confirmed a date, and it remains unclear whether the company will hold an event or announce the products through its website and press releases.
An October event would not be unprecedented. Apple held its “Scary Fast” event on October 30, 2023, and its “Unleashed” event on October 18, 2021.






What could Apple launch at the next event?
The rumored lineup centers on Apple’s first smart-home display, often called HomePad. Gurman describes a 6-inch screen mounted above a speaker base on a manually tilting arm, plus a separate wall-mounted version. Updated HomePod mini and Apple TV 4K models with faster processors are also expected.
Other rumored launches include new iPads and a touchscreen MacBook Pro, but this report does not establish that they will arrive alongside the smart-home products.





Apple event calendar 2026: What has Apple launched this year?


TimescaleEvent themeDatesProducts

March Special Experience2-4 MarchLaunched: iPhone 17e, MacBooks Neo, Pro & Air, iPad Air
JuneWWDCJune 8Unveiled plans for: iOS, macOS, other software, AI and Siri
SeptemberiPhone eventSeptember 9Launched: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone Duo, new Apple Watch, AirPods 5
OctoberRumored smart-home launchOctober 13 (rumored)Possible: HomePad, HomePod mini, Apple TV
Late 2026Other possible announcementsUnconfirmedPossible: Touchscreen MacBook, iPads
Spring 2027TBCTBCExpected: iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, iPhone Air 2

 



Apple has held three events so far in 2026, although the first was not an event in the traditional sense. On March 4, the company invited select media to hands-on “experiences” in multiple locations. In the run-up to that date, Apple launched several products via press release, including the iPhone 17e, M4 iPad Air, and M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro, M5 MacBook Air and the MacBook Neo.
The second event was WWDC, which began with a keynote on June 8. At the WWDC keynote Apple outlined the upcoming changes to its operating systems, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate.
In August Apple issued press releases to announce the new Mac mini and Mac Studio. 
At the September 9 event Apple unveiled the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, a foldable iPhone Duo, a new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. 

				
					

				
			
Here’s when the 2026 Apple events might take place.

Foundry





 FAQ 


1.
How far in advance does Apple announce an event?
Apple usually announces its events around one to two weeks before they take place, although the timing varies. That means an October event could still be announced fairly late in the month. Apple may also choose not to hold an event at all and instead unveil new products through press releases, as it has done with a number of recent Mac and iPad launches.





2.
What time does the next Apple event start in U.S., U.K. and other global time zones
Apple keynotes usually start at 10 am PT. A future event would likely follow the same pattern. That translates to the following times in the countries where most of our readers live:
U.S.: 10 am PDT, 11 am MDT, 12 pm CDT, 1 pm EDT
Canada: as above, plus 2 pm ADT
U.K.: 6 pm
Europe: 7 pm CEST, 8 pm EEST
India: 10:30 pm IST
Australia: next day — 1 am AWST, 2:30 am ACST, 3 am AEST
New Zealand: next day — 5 am NZST
The timings are generally the same for all Apple Keynotes, but can be slightly different if Apple holds the event during the period of a couple of weeks when the clocks have changed in the U.S. but not elsewhere (in 2026 the clocks will change in the U.S. on November 1, while in the U.K. they change on October 25).
Sometimes Apple holds events at different times, for example, in October 2023 the event was held in late afternoon in San Francisco, which meant it was midnight in the U.K. 
If Apple doesn’t hold an event and instead just issues a press release, that usually happens around 8 am PT, 11 am ET and 4 pm U.K. time.





3.
How long do Apple events usually last?
Apple keynotes usually last between one and two hours and feature the CEO alongside various other Apple executives. With John Ternus succeeding Tim Cook as CEO on September 1, 2026, this will be his first major product keynote in the role.
WWDC and the September event tend to be longer keynotes; the spring and late-fall events can be slightly shorter.
For example, the September 2024 event was 1 hour 38 minutes.





4.
How often does Apple hold events?
There can be as many as four Apple events in a year:  
Spring Event
WWDC in June
iPhone Event in September
Late Fall Event in October
This event calendar is by no means set in stone, though, with the spring and October events being less regular. Some years, Apple doesn’t hold a spring event at all. In 2025 Apple only held two events, preferring instead to announce new products via press release.





5.
Does Apple take part in other events?
Apple doesn’t participate in major industry trade shows such as CES and IFA. Instead Apple invites the press and industry professionals to Apple Park to hear all about its latest products and services. Apple calls these ‘events’ and it streams them live online to millions of viewers.





6.
Does Apple ever announce products without an event? 
Apple frequently announces products without a keynote event, often opting for press releases or multi-day announcement windows. In recent years, the company has increasingly reserved its large-scale media events for major flagship launches, such as the primary iPhone lineup in September, while using press releases for iterative updates or “chip bumps” that may not warrant a full hour-long presentation.





7.
How to watch an Apple event
Apple events are typically broadcast across several digital platforms, allowing viewers to tune in from almost any device. While the company previously restricted access to its own hardware or the Safari browser, these barriers have been removed in recent years.
You can access live Apple presentations through the following official channels:
YouTube: This is often considered the easiest way to watch. Apple streams its keynotes live on its official YouTube channel, which can be accessed via any web browser or the YouTube app on smartphones, tablets, and smart TVs.
Apple.com: The company hosts a dedicated “Events” page on its official website. For the best experience on a PC, it is recommended to use Microsoft Edge on Windows 10 or later.
Apple TV App: The stream is available within the Apple TV app on iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple TV hardware. Keynotes are usually listed in the app’s lineup a day or two before the event begins.
Apple Podcasts: Apple also showcases its events through the Podcasts app on Apple devices, where you can watch the video presentation.
You may also like to tune in to our Live Blog which will provide minute-by-minute text updates and analysis as products are announced.
Following the end of the event, detailed breakdowns will also be available on the Macworld Podcast, which can be found on Spotify, Soundcloud, and Apple Podcasts. 








Will Apple have a second fall event in 2026?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Will there be a late fall event in 2026?
The latest reporting points to a smart-home launch on October 13, although its presentation format remains unclear. Apple could announce these products without holding a keynote.
The last time Apple held a late fall event was on October 30, 2023, and before that on October 18, 2021. So while a late fall event would not be unprecedented, it has become relatively uncommon.
Right now, there is no way of knowing whether Apple will hold another event in late 2026, or whether it will continue to launch new products through press releases instead. In the past, October events have often focused on Macs, but in recent years Apple has shown that it does not always consider a dedicated event necessary for Mac launches.
What could Apple launch at the late fall 2026 event?
Apple’s next launch could focus on smart-home products, including the rumored HomePad display, an updated HomePod mini and a new Apple TV 4K. The latter two are expected to feature faster processors that could support Siri AI features.
Other possible launches before the end of the year include the rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro and updates to the iPad and iPad mini. However, it remains unclear whether Apple would announce these alongside its smart-home products, hold a separate event or introduce them through press releases.
For more information about Apple’s late fall events, read: Apple’s October Event: Date, time and what will launch.






Will Apple hold a spring event in 2027? 

				
					

				
			John Ternus: Apple’s new CEO.
Michael Simon / Foundry




Apple’s spring events have become increasingly unpredictable. The company has not held a traditional spring event since May 2024, although it did invite members of the media, including Macworld, to a “Special Apple Experience” in 2026. 
Rather than a keynote presentation, the March 4, 2026 gathering was a hands-on showcase that followed three days of product announcements, including the MacBook Neo, iPhone 17e, and M5 MacBook Air.
Will Apple take a similar approach to spring product launches in 2027? It’s certainly possible. The format appeared to work well, allowing each product announcement to receive its own media coverage rather than competing for attention during a single event. 
Apple is expected to release three iPhone models in spring 2027 – or it could be two new iPhones, with the Air and iPhone 18 merging.
iPhone 18 (base model)
iPhone 18e
iPhone Air 2
Apple may also update the MacBook Air with an M6 processor in spring 2027. 






When is WWDC 2027?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




When is the WWDC keynote?
In 2026 the WWDC keynote was on Monday June 8. In 2025 it started on Monday June 9. We expect WWDC will start on Monday 7 June in 2027. 
WWDC generally runs from the Monday to Friday in the second week of June. 
What Apple could launch at WWDC
WWDC is Apple’s big developer event at which it reveals plans for the operating systems that run on Apple hardware.
In June 2027 we expect Apple to unveil details of iOS 28, iPadOS 28, macOS 28, updates to watchOS, tvOS, HomePod software, and an update to Apple’s realityOS.
Apple sometimes announces new hardware at WWDC, usually the high-end models targeted at power users, so we could see new Macs.
Following the keynote on Monday, developer events and sessions will run throughout the week. You can read more about WWDC date, times and everything you need to know in a separate article.






What did Apple launch at past events?
So far in 2026 Apple has held an ‘experience’, which rather than being an event in the traditional sense, was a chance for journalists to get a look at products Apple had launched in the days prior, including MacBook Neo and iPhone 17e. The company also hosted the WWDC keynote on June 8, at which it revealed its plans for Apple Intelligence and Siri in iOS 27, macOS 27 and the other operating systems. Plus Apple held its iPhone launch event on September 9 at which the iPhone 18 Pro and Max, iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and AirPods 5 launched. 
In 2025 Apple only held two events. The first was its Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC) on June 9, at which it introduced the new features coming in the next version of its operating systems, and the second was the huge September 9 Apple Event where it launched new Apple Watches, new AirPods Pro and the new iPhones for 2025.
Apple doesn’t have to hold an event to launch new products though. Prior to WWDC, Apple launched a new iPhone 16e via press release on February 19, a new iPad and iPad Air via press release on March 4, and a new MacBook Air and Mac Studio on March 5. 
Apple then went on to launch a new M5 MacBook Pro and M5 iPad Pro in October. No event was held to mark these launches.
In 2024, Apple held three events: one on Tuesday, May 7, at which it launched new iPads; a keynote to kick off WWDC on June 10; and an event on September 9 at which Apple unveiled the new iPhone 16, Apple Watch Series 10 and the AirPods 4. In October 2024 there was no event, but Apple did announce new products (iMac, Mac mini and MacBook Pro) via press release.
In 2023 there were three events: WWDC in June, an iPhone event in September, and Apple’s second fall event on October 30 (or after midnight on October 31 if you weren’t in the U.S.).
In 2022 Apple held three events: a spring event on March 8, WWDC on June 6, and the iPhone 14 launch on September 7. In other years Apple has held four events though.

title: Apple's Smart Home Hub: Everything We Know So Far
content:
Apple is working on a new smart home accessory that will serve as a hub for interacting with Siri AI, controlling HomeKit devices, watching videos, checking the calendar and the weather, and generally offering up useful information to everyone in the household. 


This guide aggregates everything that we know about Apple's smart home hub.

Design

Apple's smart home device will somewhat resemble an iPad, and it will have a display-focused design. It is expected to be square rather than rectangular, and it will measure in at 6 inches with quarter-inch black bezels around the edges.

In terms of size, it will look similar to two iPhones that are side-by-side, and it will be about as thick as an iPhone. Apple imagines people having multiples of the hub in different rooms of the house. The device will support touch input for opening apps and controlling connected devices.


Apple is making two versions of the home hub. One will have a 6-inch display and is meant to be mounted on the wall, and the second version has the same 6-inch display and a hemispherical speaker base that looks similar to the iMac G4. The display attaches to the base with a polished metal arm that holds the small screen and allows it to be tilted forward or backward. The base features speaker hole perforations and a rubber bottom for stability. 

The original ‌iMac‌ G4

The wall-mounted version will have a thin square base for the speakers and the mics, and it will sit flush against the wall. Both models will have a 1080p camera on the front for FaceTime calls, authenticating users, and recognizing different people in the home. Apple is planning to release the hub in a gray aluminum finish.

The device has no internal battery and is instead meant to be used while connected to power via USB-C. 

Sensors

The smart home hub will be able to determine how close a person is standing to it, adjusting features from there. When no one is nearby, for example, it might show the temperature, but as someone approaches, it could shift to an interface for adjusting the thermostat.

recognize hand gestures for longer-range control. 

Facial recognition

The home hub will use a Face ID-like feature along with voice for authentication and to identify who is in a room. With the recognition features, the home hub will be able to switch to the profile for the person in the home who is interacting with the device. Each user will have a customizable profile and interface with options to change profiles through the Control Center. 

Face ID, so voice is an alternative. Apple's HomePod also uses voice recognition for some personalized features. Users will be able to set up secondary authentication with an iPhone for more security, and a visitor mode will hide personal information.

Rumors suggest there is a Mac-style edge light around the screen to offer lighting so the device can identify people in the dark. 

Chip

Apple's smart home accessory is expected to use an A18 chip or better for Apple Intelligence support. Given that ‌Apple Intelligence‌ requires 8GB RAM minimum, it will have at least 8GB RAM.

Operating System

Apple's home hub will run an operating system that Apple refers to as "Charismatic" internally, though it could be called homeOS when it launches. It's going to use elements from tvOS, watchOS, and iOS, and it will sync with the iPhone for setup purposes. 

Interface

Apple does not plan to create a dedicated App Store for the home hub, but it will come with several apps pre-installed. The main view will be a customizable home screen with widgets that can show the weather, important home controls, photo slideshows, upcoming events, and more. A built-in camera will scan the face of each user, bringing up different apps and a Home Screen for each person.

The interface is something like a cross between watchOS and the iPhone's StandBy mode, with a heavy focus on clock faces and photo slideshows when the device is idle. The ‌Home Screen‌ will feature Apple Watch-like icons, but the apps will have an iPad-like design with a two-panel layout. There will be familiar customization options like pressing and holding to rearrange icons and swiping up to get to the app launcher. 

Widgets shown on the device from an iPhone that's connected will only display widget content when the primary user is in the home. A Smart Stack will be available to intelligently rotate through different widget options throughout the day, and the clock will be customizable with a Face Gallery.

The hub will adopt the visual aesthetic of ‌Siri‌ AI, with darker design elements. A software-based dock will be available for launching apps, and the hub will be built around ‌Siri‌ AI. 

Apps

Several Apple apps will be installed even though there won't be a dedicated ‌App Store‌. Apps that are rumored:

 
Safari

 
Apple News

 
Apple Music

 
Apple Podcasts

 
Notes

 
Calendar

 
Photos

 
Home

Messages

Reminders

‌FaceTime‌



The hub will support integration into ‌HomeKit‌ scenes alongside other smart home products, and it will play videos, so it can be used for things like following along with a recipe when in the kitchen. 

Intercom

More than one of the devices can be used throughout the home, and two or more can serve as room-to-room intercoms.

AirPlay

With its built-in speakers, the device will support music playback and it will be able to work as an AirPlay receiver.

homeOS Trademark

Apple appears to be using a shell company to trademark "homeOS" in several countries around the world, with the trademarking kicking off in October 2024. Apple has secured the homeOS trademark in Liechtenstein, and trademarks are pending in the U.S., Argentina, Peru, and more. 

Future Smart Home Accessories

Apple is creating an indoor security camera that will connect to the home hub, and it's rumored for 2027. Privacy would be a focus, providing an alternative to cameras from companies like Ring and Nest.

Pricing

Apple's home hub could be priced somewhere around $350, which would make it more expensive than competing products like the Amazon Echo Show. 

Launch Date

Apple's smart home hub is rumored to be debuting on October 13 alongside a new Apple TV 4K and a new HomePod mini.

title: iPhone 18 Pro speakers ‘crackling and popping,’ some owners complain
content:
Macworld





It’s been just 12 days since the iPhone 18 Pro went on sale, and some customers are already complaining about their phones. Specifically, at certain times the speakers produce a clicking, crackling, snapping, or “raspy” sound.
As is often the case with such issues, affected parties congregated on a Reddit thread to discuss the problem.
The original poster reports that shortly after setup their new iPhone 18 Pro Max produced a brief clicking or popping noise from the speaker (either upper or lower; the poster seems unclear on this) “almost as if someone is pulling out an aux cord.” This didn’t just happen once. It happened, they report, a number of times “during app switching and [while] playing around with volume and possibly voice dictation.” But it became less frequent over time, and didn’t happen at all in the few hours before the post was made.
In a later edit, they add that “music at high volume sounds raspy as well.”
At the time of writing, there are 29 direct, undeleted and non-mod replies to the post, and by my count at least 21 of these say they’ve experienced the same issue(s). Some report positive conclusions. One says it only happened on phone calls and that since updating to iOS 27.0.1 has stopped entirely. Another says that going into the Phone settings and choosing “Standard” mode rather than “Voice Isolation” led to “way less crackling.”
But some cases appear to be more severe. One commenter, translated from Vietnamese, complains that they “hear random clicking or crackling sounds almost whenever I interact with the screen. Sometimes, I even hear it the moment I touch the screen to wake it up.”
More reports of the issue have appeared on the MacRumors forum. Again, complaints are made about “crackling” sounds, “intermittent popping sounds,” a “super faint tick/pop from the earpiece speaker,” and a different, “very unpleasant” emphasis in the higher frequencies, as compared to the iPhone 17 Pro Max. And again, far too many commenters confirm that they’ve experienced the same issue for this to be dismissed as user error or a single defective unit.
Apple has not yet made a public statement about the issue, but may address it in a software update. Go into Settings and select General > Software Update and follow the prompts to install the latest version of iOS.
Since Apple just released iOS 27.0.1 this week to fix other iPhone 18 Pro launch bugs, however, an imminent update is not guaranteed. In the meantime we recommend that owners of affected phones contact Apple to get them fixed, especially before the two-week return period ends.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman today reported that Apple plans to unveil its all-new smart home hub, a second-generation HomePod mini, and a new Apple TV 4K model on October 13, the same date that Gruber mentioned in his speculative piece a few days ago.

separate post, Gruber opined that there is "no way" that Apple would unveil the home hub through an Apple Newsroom announcement only, given it is an all-new device with an all-new interface. title: New macOS malware masquerades as Zoom installer
content:
Macworld





Jamf Threat Labs has posted a report on new malware that attacks macOS. The malware installer presents itself as a Zoom installer that actually installs the app, but it also installs an infostealer dubbed CloudSyncD that works in the background to capture data and send it to the attacker.
The installation is presented as an app icon that is dragged to the macOS Applications folder, a common method of installation. However, because the malware lacks the proper signatures, macOS’s Gatekeeper will not allow it to run. To bypass Gatekeeper, the installer window has a background image with instructions for the user on how to override Gatekeeper.

				
					

				
			Jamf Threat Labs
The installation of the app appears legitimate and mounts as a disk image named Zoom laid out to look like any ordinary Mac installer with the application icon on the left and an alias to the Applications folder on the right. However, it also includes user instructions to bypass macOS’ Gatekeeper security,
If CloudSyncD is installed, it monitors and records data that the user has entered. It can send reports to the attackers as frequently as every 8 seconds. CloudSyncD can also be used be the attacker to remotely execute commands.
How to protect yourself from malware
The easiest way to protect yourself from malware is to avoid downloading software from unfamiliar repositories. Apple has vetted software in the Mac App Store, and it is the safest way to get apps. If you prefer not to patronize the Mac App Store, then buy software directly from the developer and their website. If you insist on using cracked software, you will always risk malware exposure.
Never open links in emails or texts you receive from unknown and unexpected sources. If you get a message that looks like it is from an entity that you do business with, check the sender’s email address and inspect the URL carefully. If you see a link or button, you can Control-click it, select Copy Link Address, and then paste it into a text editor to see the actual URL and check it.
Macworld has several guides to help, including a guide on whether or not you need antivirus software, a list of Mac viruses, malware, and trojans, and a comparison of Mac security software.

title: Best AirPods 2026: Which AirPods should you buy?
content:
Macworld





Apple’s AirPods lineup falls into three main families: the AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2.
For most buyers, the choice is between the AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3. AirPods 5 start at $129 and combine an open-ear design with Active Noise Cancellation, while the $249 AirPods Pro 3 use foam-infused silicone tips for a more secure fit and stronger noise isolation, and add heart-rate sensing and Apple’s hearing-health features.
AirPods Max 2 are a different proposition: $549 over-ear headphones aimed at buyers who prioritize sound quality and noise cancellation and specifically prefer an over-ear design.
In this guide, we compare Apple’s current AirPods lineup to explain the key differences between each model and help you decide which is best for you. We look at design and fit, noise cancellation, sound, battery life, health and hearing features, and price, as well as whether it’s worth considering older AirPods at a discount. We also compare AirPods 5 directly with AirPods Pro 3 and explain which AirPods offer the best value for different types of buyer.


Which AirPods are the best?
We recommend AirPods Pro 3 as the best AirPods overall, thanks to their combination of noise cancellation, secure fit, longer battery life and additional health features.
For many people, however, AirPods 5 will be the better buy. They now include Active Noise Cancellation, Adaptive Audio, Transparency mode and Conversation Awareness, closing much of the feature gap with the Pro model while costing substantially less. They’re also the obvious choice if you prefer an open fit rather than silicone ear tips.
AirPods Max 2 are best considered separately. They are over-ear headphones rather than earbuds and cost more than twice as much as AirPods Pro 3, so they make most sense for buyers specifically looking for that style of headphone.

Best for: Buyers who want the strongest combination of ANC, fit, battery life and features.
Buy AirPods Pro 3 if: You want the best noise cancellation of Apple’s earbuds, longer battery life, a secure in-ear fit or the health and hearing features.
Don’t buy AirPods Pro 3 if: You dislike earbuds that seal the ear canal or don’t need enough of their extra features to justify spending $100–$120 more than on AirPods 5.
For most buyers who don’t object to silicone ear tips, AirPods Pro 3 are the best AirPods you can buy.
Released in September 2025, the third-generation AirPods Pro improved on an already excellent pair of earbuds without increasing the $249 launch price. In our review, Jason Cross praised their more comfortable and secure fit, improved battery life, better noise cancellation and Transparency mode, and effective heart-rate sensor. Taken together, those apparently small changes add up to a significant improvement.
The biggest physical change is the fit. AirPods Pro 3 have redesigned earbuds with foam-infused tips available in five sizes, including XXS. In our testing, they stayed securely in place even during intense activity and felt more comfortable than the previous generation.
Noise cancellation is another major advantage. Apple says AirPods Pro 3 remove twice as much noise as AirPods Pro 2, while our review also found improvements to noise reduction, Transparency mode and bass response.
Battery life is strong too. Apple rates the earbuds for up to eight hours with ANC enabled, an estimate that was broadly borne out in our testing. The charging case takes total ANC listening time to up to 24 hours.
AirPods Pro 3 also have features the AirPods 5 don’t. The built-in heart-rate sensor works with workouts in the Fitness app, while Apple’s Hearing Test, Hearing Aid and Hearing Protection features make the Pro model particularly compelling for users interested in hearing health.

Don’t buy AirPods 5 if: Maximum isolation and noise cancellation are important, or you want heart-rate sensing and Apple’s hearing-health features.
AirPods 5 are no longer simply the cheaper AirPods that miss out on most of the Pro features.
Apple introduced AirPods 5 in September 2026 with Active Noise Cancellation as standard. That immediately makes the decision more interesting: you can now get open-ear AirPods with ANC for $129, compared with $249 for AirPods Pro 3.
Like previous standard AirPods, they don’t use silicone ear tips. They sit in the ear without sealing the ear canal, which will be an important advantage for anyone who finds AirPods Pro uncomfortable or dislikes the isolated feeling of in-ear earbuds.
Noise cancellation is much improved. Apple says AirPods 5 remove up to 50 percent more external noise than AirPods 4 with ANC, thanks to a redesigned acoustic architecture and updated computational audio. Macworld also notes that Transparency mode has been improved and that Adaptive Audio can automatically blend ANC and Transparency according to your surroundings.
Sound has been upgraded too, with a new acoustic design and next-generation Adaptive EQ intended to improve performance across a wider range of ear shapes.
There are actually two AirPods 5 packages, but unlike the previous generation they don’t differ in whether ANC is included.
The $129 AirPods 5 come with a USB-C charging case. Apple rates these for up to four hours of listening with ANC enabled or six hours with noise control turned off, and up to 20 hours with the case when using ANC.
The $149 AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case are the more compelling option. They can charge over USB-C, with an Apple Watch charger or with a Qi charger, and the case includes a speaker for Find My. They also add volume adjustment by swiping the stem. Battery life rises to as much as five hours with ANC, seven hours with noise control off and 22 hours with the case when using ANC.
At only $20 more, we’d lean toward the Wireless Charging Case version unless you’re particularly keen to keep the price down.

Best for: Apple users who specifically want premium over-ear headphones.
Buy AirPods Max 2 if: You want over-ear headphones, excellent sound and ANC, and particularly value AirPods integration with Apple devices.
Don’t buy AirPods Max 2 if: Price, weight or portability are important. AirPods Pro 3 offer many of the same AirPods features for less than half the price.
AirPods Max 2 are the choice for buyers who specifically want Apple’s over-ear headphones rather than earbuds.
Apple introduced AirPods Max 2 in March 2026, finally replacing the original AirPods Max with a model powered by the H2 chip. The change brought features including Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Voice Isolation and Live Translation to the AirPods Max line.
Sound quality remains excellent. Our review also rated the Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency mode among the model’s strongest attributes. Apple says ANC is up to 1.5 times more effective than on the previous generation.
They also support lossless and ultra-low-latency audio over USB-C.
But AirPods Max 2 still come with significant compromises. They weigh 13.6 ounces, and our reviewer found that weight noticeable when moving around. Apple also retained the controversial Smart Case and the unusual power-management system that means the headphones can’t simply be switched off manually.
Battery life is rated at up to 20 hours with ANC enabled.
And then there’s the price. AirPods Max 2 cost $549, making them more than twice the price of AirPods Pro 3. Our review consequently found them difficult to recommend despite their excellent sound, ANC and Apple ecosystem integration.

AirPods 5 vs AirPods Pro 3: Which should you buy?

				
					

				
			
AirPods Pro 3 vs AirPods 5

Foundry





AirPods 5 are better if…
You dislike earbuds that seal your ear canal.
You want to spend less.
An open fit is more important than maximum noise isolation.
You want ANC but don’t need the Pro health features.
AirPods Pro 3 are better if…
You want Apple’s hearing-health features.
Strong noise cancellation is a priority.
You want longer battery life.
You want a more secure in-ear fit.
You want heart-rate sensing.
The difference between standard AirPods and AirPods Pro used to be straightforward: standard AirPods were cheaper and open-fitting, while the Pros added ANC and Apple’s more sophisticated listening modes.
With the AirPods 5, that distinction is less clear. Both AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 use Apple’s H2 chip and support Active Noise Cancellation, Adaptive Audio, Transparency mode, Conversation Awareness, Voice Isolation and Personalized Spatial Audio.
The remaining differences are nevertheless significant.
Design and fit
AirPods 5 use an open-ear design and don’t use ear tips. AirPods Pro 3 sit more tightly in the ear canal and come with foam-infused silicone tips in five sizes. When we reviewed the AirPods Pro 3 we found the redesigned tips substantially improved comfort and security and kept the earbuds in place during strenuous exercise.
Choose AirPods 5 if you don’t like the plugged-ear sensation of silicone tips.
Choose AirPods Pro 3 if you want a tighter, more secure fit and better isolation.
Noise cancellation
AirPods 5 include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, unlike AirPods 4, which were sold with or without ANC. But their open-ear design means they approach noise reduction differently from the AirPods Pro 3.
AirPods Pro 3 use ear tips to create a seal in the ear canal, giving them a natural advantage when it comes to isolation. Apple says their ANC removes up to twice as much noise as AirPods Pro 2, and in our testing both noise cancellation and Transparency mode were improved over the previous generation.
AirPods 5 don’t create a seal, but their open-ear ANC is significantly more effective than before. Apple says they remove up to 50 percent more external noise than AirPods 4 with ANC.
AirPods 5 are the better choice if you dislike the feeling of a sealed in-ear fit.
AirPods Pro 3 remain the better choice if maximum noise reduction and isolation are your priorities.
Battery life
AirPods Pro 3 have a significant battery advantage. They last up to eight hours with ANC enabled and up to 24 hours including the charging case.
The $129 AirPods 5 manage up to four hours with ANC, while the $149 Wireless Charging Case version increases that to five hours.
That’s a substantial difference if you frequently use your AirPods for long journeys or extended listening sessions.
AirPods 5 = 4 hours battery life 
AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case = 5 hours battery life
AirPods Pro 3 = 8 hours battery life
Health and hearing features
The AirPods Pro 3 include a heart-rate sensor that can measure your heart rate during workouts, and our reviewer found the results comparable to an Apple Watch during testing.
They also support Apple’s Hearing Test, Hearing Aid and Hearing Protection features.
Those features aren’t available on AirPods 5.
AirPods Pro 3 are also the obvious choice if Apple’s health features are important.
Price
The Pro model costs $100 more than the AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case and $120 more than the cheapest version.
The gap can shrink during sales. AirPods Pro 3 fell as low as $169 during Amazon Prime Day in June 2026, so it’s always worth checking the live price comparison before deciding.
AirPods 5 start at $129, or $149 with the Wireless Charging Case.
AirPods Pro 3 are $249.


						

							


Which AirPods 5 should you get? 
Unlike AirPods 4, Apple doesn’t sell one AirPods 5 model with ANC and another without it. All AirPods 5 have Active Noise Cancellation.
Instead, the choice is between cases.
The $129 model has a USB-C charging case. It offers up to four hours of battery life with ANC and up to 20 hours including the case.
For $149, the Wireless Charging Case can also charge using an Apple Watch charger or Qi charger and includes a speaker for Find My. The earbuds in this package also support volume adjustment by swiping the stems. Battery life increases to five hours with ANC and 22 hours with the case.
Our recommendation: Buy the version with wireless charging case – given the relatively small $20 difference, the $149 version is the better buy for most people.


						

							


Should you buy older AirPods?
We’d generally recommend buying the latest generation rather than deliberately seeking out older AirPods because there is a considerable gap between the different generations. 
Should you buy AirPods 4?
AirPods 5 start at the same $129 MSRP previously charged for AirPods 4 without ANC, but now include ANC as standard, along with improved noise cancellation and sound quality.
That makes AirPods 4 difficult to recommend unless you find them at a substantial clearance discount. They dropped to $99 during Prime Day 2026, but with AirPods 5 now available at $129, we’d want to see them priced noticeably lower than that.
Our recommendation: Only buy AirPods 4 at a steep discount.
$89 at  Walmart										 | 
																$149 at  B&H										 | 
																$149.99 at  Best Buy						
					
Should you buy AirPods Pro 2?
AirPods Pro 2 remain capable earbuds, but AirPods Pro 3 improve the fit, noise cancellation and battery life, while adding heart-rate sensing.
If you find AirPods Pro 2 at a heavy discount, they can still make sense. But the closer their price gets to a discounted pair of AirPods Pro 3, the harder they are to recommend.
Our recommendation: Only buy AirPods Pro 2 at a significant discount and if you don’t need heart-rate sensing.
Should you buy the original AirPods Max?
AirPods Max 2 retain many aspects of the original design but add the H2 chip, which enables Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Voice Isolation and Live Translation. ANC has also been improved.
If you’re going to spend close to AirPods Max money, the second-generation model is therefore the one to get.
Our recommendation: Only buy if the discount is substantial.

 FAQ 


1.
What’s the difference between AirPods and AirPods Pro?
The biggest difference is fit. AirPods 5 use an open-ear design, while AirPods Pro 3 use foam-infused silicone tips that seal the ear canal.
Both now have Active Noise Cancellation, Adaptive Audio, Transparency mode and Conversation Awareness. AirPods Pro 3 nevertheless offer stronger isolation, longer ANC battery life and exclusive features including heart-rate sensing, Hearing Test, Hearing Aid and Hearing Protection.
AirPods 5 start at $129; AirPods Pro 3 cost $249.





2.
Do AirPods work with Macs and iPads?
Yes. AirPods work particularly well with Apple devices.
Once your AirPods are paired, they can automatically connect to devices associated with your Apple account, and Automatic Device Switching can move playback between devices depending on what you’re using.
Apple lists current versions of macOS and iPadOS among the supported platforms for AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2.





3.
Can you use AirPods with non-Apple devices?
Yes. AirPods are Bluetooth headphones and can be used with non-Apple hardware.
We have, for example, demonstrated how AirPods can be paired directly with a Nintendo Switch using its Bluetooth Audio settings.
Apple also explicitly states that current AirPods can be used as Bluetooth headphones with non-Apple devices, although some functionality may be limited.
The main reason to use AirPods with Apple hardware is therefore the deeper ecosystem integration rather than basic Bluetooth compatibility.





4.
Do AirPods have Find My?
Yes, but the capabilities depend on the model and case.
AirPods can be located through Apple’s Find My system. The $149 AirPods 5 Wireless Charging Case includes a speaker for Find My alerts, while the standard $129 USB-C case does not. AirPods Pro 3 also include a speaker in their MagSafe charging case.
Find My support is useful not just for locating misplaced AirPods but also when checking whether a suspicious pair of AirPods behaves as genuine Apple hardware. See our guide to spotting fake AirPods for more advice.





5.
Are AirPods waterproof?
No. AirPods aren’t “waterproof”, but they do offer some water resistance. 
AirPods 5 are rated IP57 for dust, sweat and water resistance. AirPods Pro 3 and their charging case are also rated IP57.
That makes them suitable for exercise and provides protection against water exposure, but water resistance isn’t the same thing as waterproofing and shouldn’t be taken as an invitation to use them for swimming.
AirPods Max 2 don’t have a water-resistance rating.

Apple's custom-designed N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support.

  
Apple's custom-designed C1X or C2 modem for cellular configurations.

  
A redesigned speaker system with no speaker holes and potentially an iPhone earpiece-like speaker in the top bezel.

  
IP-rated water resistance for the first time.



an October launch most likely. In the U.S., the current iPad mini starts at $599 after receiving a $100 price increase in June, which Apple attributed to skyrocketing RAM and storage chip prices. With a costlier OLED display, the next model might be even more expensive.

title: This $46 burgundy charger and cable is perfect for your iPhone 18 Pro
content:
Macworld





		
Baseus PicoGo Pro AH22
View Deal
Even if you didn’t buy a new iPhone 18 Pro, you’re probably feeling the new Burgundy color. Well you can get it on the hot new trend with this three-port Baseus PicoGo Pro AH22 100W charger that’s 23 percent off at Amazon. Instead of $60, you’ll only pay $46, and you’ll even get a free $13 100W color-matched cable when you add both to your chart, a total savings of $27.
We’re not going to lie, but the color is a big part of the appeal for this particular charger. This is the Dark Cherry Edition, which is basically the same shade as the Burgundy finish of the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. If you just picked up one of those phones, your charger and cable can finally match it. A black version is also available for a couple of bucks less, but this one is really a looker.
Beyond the hot color, this charger is super fast and can handle your smartphone, earbuds, and laptop all at once. There are three USB-C ports available, and with up to 100W of total output, it won’t stumble through your charge. The charger is smart enough to handle the power split on its own, sending each device the amount of power it needs. You don’t have to think about which port goes where. Just plug in and go. The interactive smart display will show you exactly how much power is going through every port, temperature, charging time, and more.
The size makes this Baseus PicoGo Pro charger a perfect travel companion, too, measuring just 54 x 52 x 32 mm. That’s about as small as an AirPods case. It also helps that the prongs fold flat so they won’t scratch out your tech or snag on clothes in your bag.
For $46 with a free $13 cable, this is an easy pick if you want one pocket-sized charger that handles all your devices and matches your new iPhone.
